en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery:

As for controlling the path of return and encompassing all things, or treading upon the essential ultimate and rectifying one’s endeavors—nothing surpasses alerting the ten perfections within a single act of giving and dispelling the six obscurations through the three types of *dāna*. This is especially true regarding the grand doctrine of Prajñā.

He indeed commands the whole with a lofty gaze; he is truly the bolted door and the window for the multitude’s minds, and the pivotal axis for the accumulation of virtuous conduct. Thus, he is able to encompass the ultimate reality and fill the dusty realms of the world.

To expand upon it, there are no conditions; to settle it, there is no movement. Great Compassion raises its head, and Great Renunciation supports its tail; one calmly cultivates the suffering of the five pains and swiftly traverses the vast sequence of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
May there be no distinction between near and far, so that whatever is encountered may serve as a resource for practice;
may there be no distinction between great and small, so that wherever one treads, the path shall surely flourish.

To rely upon the formless throughout the eternal day, and to cease the wheel of existence within the long night—to exhaust all obscurity and perfect all subtlety—is this not the ultimate realization of Prajñā?

There is a Heavenly King who is the most supreme; he renounced the pleasures of his palace to descend and pay homage, and spread his illustrious name upward as a tribute. With every thought focused upon this, he investigated and deliberated.
However, because our positions are far apart and the Way is obstructed, it cannot be preserved through direct observation;
therefore, to guide the multitude and harmonize with the celestial cycles, I rely on words to provide an exhortation and bring about awakening.
This is the previously existing *Śrīdevīprajñāpāramitāsūtra*, now translated into eight fascicles and seventeen chapters.
In elucidating the grand principles and unlocking the profound barriers, the treasures of the Dharma have indeed shone forth in profusion and the groves of meaning have accumulated in abundance.
The three types of self-nature are densely interwoven with the non-substantiality of nature;
the myriad regions of the fruit-virtues are profoundly manifest, radiant despite the absence of a personal agent.
Even those scholars who open their cases and study the texts still rarely find a teacher to verify their understanding;
how much more so for a traveler who rides upon a cup—how could he not reflect upon this?
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: On Dependent Origination, Part Six. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying on the summit of Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, together with a great saṃgha of forty-two thousand bhikṣus.
All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions;
they had attained true mastery, with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated, like well-trained thoroughbred horses.
Like great dragons, they have done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished;
having laid down all heavy burdens and attained their own welfare, they have exhausted the fetters of existence and are liberated through right knowledge.

They have reached the supreme perfection of mastery over the mind—with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remains alone on the stage of training and has attained the fruit of stream-entry—namely, the Venerable Aññā-Koṇḍañña.
Then Mahākāśyapa, Guptabhadra, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, MahāMudgala, Mahākātyāyana, Pilindavatsa, Śāriputra,
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Bakula, Upāli, Rāhula, Aniruddha, and Subhūti—
He was the leader.

Furthermore, there were seventy-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had all thoroughly penetrated the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā), whose conduct was harmonious and easy to transform, who practiced with equanimity, and who had attained the dharani-door of unimpeded eloquence. All...
A truly pure and virtuous spiritual friend for sentient beings, capable of turning the subtle and wondrous Wheel of Dharma that never regresses;

one who out of compassion for the world protects and upholds the treasury of the Dharma; one who has already made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas; one who succeeds and exalts the Triple Gem so that it remains uninterrupted;
one who has thoroughly penetrated the profound realm of all Buddhas; a true son of the Dharma King bound to only one more birth.
They are always able to succeed the Buddhas in turning the wheel of the true Dharma; though dwelling in the world, they remain unstained by it.

Possessing such immeasurable merits as these, they come from this buddha-field or from other directions to the presence of the Buddha for the sake of hearing the Dharma—namely, the Bodhisattvas Ratilakṣaṇa, Ratnapāṇi, and Ratnamudrā.
The Bodhisattvas: Ratnaśikhin, Ratnamakuṭa, Ratnakūṭa, Ratnasāgara, Ratnārcis, Ratnadhvaja, Ratnagarbha,
Suvarṇagarbha, Viśuddhigarbha, Guṇagarbha, Samādhigarbha, and Jñānagarbha.
the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, the Bodhisattva Candragarbha, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha,
the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
the Bodhisattva Samantasvara, the Bodhisattva Samantavrata, the Bodhisattva Samantacaryā, and the Bodhisattva Samantanetra.
Sāgaramati, Vipulacakṣus, Padmanetra, Prajñā, Uttaramati, Jitamati,
Padmabuddhi, Vajrabuddhi, Sūryaprabha, Candraprabha, Jñānaprabha, and Jñānaguṇa Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Puṣpadhvaja, the Bodhisattva Sūryadarśana, the Bodhisattva Candradarśana,
the Bodhisattva Vimala, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāghoṣarāja, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, and the sixteen virtuous bodhisattvas beginning with the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha.
The Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, headed by Maitreya Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; and furthermore,
immeasurable gods of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, headed by the Four Great Kings.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, with Śakra Devendra as their chief;
and there were immeasurable gods of the Yāma Heaven, with Suyāma Devendra as their chief.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Tuṣita heavens, with King Śāntuṣita as their chief.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Nirmāṇarati heavens, with King Sunirmāṇa as their chief.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, with the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartins as their leader.
There were also immeasurable gods of the Brahmakāyika and other heavens, with Mahābrahmā as their leader.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, with Maheśvara as their leader.
These celestial kings, together with their retinues, came to the place where the Buddha was for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable asura kings—namely, the asura king Bala-vant, the asura king Dṛḍha-skandha, the asura king Citra-tejas, and the asura king Pracaṇḍa-graha—who, together with their respective retinues of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, came to the place where the Buddha was in order to hear the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable great powerful nāga kings—namely Anavatapta Nāgarāja, Caṇḍamati Nāgarāja, Sāgara-nivāsin Nāgarāja, and Śilpika Nāgarāja as their leaders—each leading immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues, who came to the place where the Buddha was for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable yakṣas, great deities, humans, non-humans, and their various retinues who came to the Buddha’s dwelling for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, the Vulture Peak Mountain, forty yojanas in length and breadth, was filled with this great assembly; there was no space left on the ground or in the air.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne, surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable great assembly; they made offerings, revered, honored, and praised him, with single-minded palms joined together, gazing up at his venerable countenance.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata manifested his supernormal powers, emitting various colored rays of light from his mouth that universally illuminated the boundless worlds of the ten directions. Having displayed these rare wonders, the light returned to the Buddha’s presence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and re-entered through his mouth.

At that time, to the east of this buddha-field, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there was a buddha-field named Adorned. There, the Buddha was named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, he currently dwells there in peace and security, proclaiming for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the true Dharma corresponding to the One Vehicle.
In that Buddha-world, even the names of the two vehicles are not heard, let alone anyone diligently practicing their respective dharmas;
all those bodhisattvas have attained non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Those sentient beings do not rely on physical food, but are sustained solely by liberation, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

That realm does not depend on the light of the sun, moon, or other luminaries; rather, the light from the Buddha’s own body constantly illuminates day and night. In that land, there are no thorns, pebbles, ravines, or mountain ridges; the ground is as level as the palm of a hand.

In that world, there was a bodhisattva named Vighuṣṭaśabda. Upon seeing this light, his mind was filled with doubt; together with a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he went before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Universal Radiance said to Vigata-āvaraṇa:

"To the west, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Gaṅgā rivers, there is a buddha-world named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni, who is fully endowed with the ten titles of a Tathāgata. He is currently expounding the Great Prajñāpāramitā for an assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is due to those causes and conditions that this auspicious omen has appeared."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva Free from Obstructions addressed him, saying:

“I now request permission to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and to listen to and receive the True Dharma; I only pray that you will grant me leave!”
Then, the Buddha Samantaprabha said to Vigatarāga, "Now is the very time; you should go at once.

Having received this permission, Vigatarāga was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately set out together with an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas and arrived at Vulture Peak. There he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.

To the south, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Pure Flower. The Buddha there is named Sunlight, fully endowed with the ten titles; in that world, there is a bodhisattva named Sun-Treasury.

To the west, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Jewel Flower. There, a Buddha named Light of Merit resides, fully endowed with the ten titles; in that world, there is a bodhisattva named Treasury of Merit.

To the north, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Pure; the Buddha there is named Sovereign King, and he has a bodhisattva named Extensive Renown.

To the southeast, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Flame-Blaze. There, a Buddha named King of Ambrosia resides, fully endowed with the ten titles; in that world, there is a bodhisattva named Non-Retrogression.

To the southwest, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Pure Merit. There, the Buddha is named Wisdom Torch, fully endowed with the ten titles; in that world, there is a bodhisattva named Great Wisdom.

To the northwest, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Pleasing; the Buddha there is named King of Wondrous Sound, who is endowed with the ten titles, and in that world there is a bodhisattva named Accumulation of Merit.

To the northeast, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Prajñālaṃkāra. The Buddha there is named Jñānottara, who is endowed with the ten titles; in that world, there is a bodhisattva named Nityapramudita.

To the north, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Acala. There, a Buddha named Vajralakṣaṇa dwells, fully endowed with the ten titles; in that world, there is a bodhisattva named Ratnadhvaja.

Below this world, passing through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Moonlight. The Buddha there is named King Adorned with Vajra Jewels, fully endowed with the ten titles; in that land, there is a bodhisattva named Precious Faith.
In this way, everything was exactly as in the eastern direction.

At that time, during the second part of the sixth chapter, "The Chapter on Thorough Comprehension," there was a celestial king named Most Victorious (*Jinvarāja*). He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have a slight doubt that I now wish to ask the Buddha; if I am granted permission, I shall venture to present my request.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Most Victorious Deva, saying:
"O Heavenly King!"
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall resolve whatever questions you may have.
Then, having received the Buddha’s permission, the Deva Varasena leaped for joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How is it that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in a single dharma, are able to penetrate all dharmas?
The Buddha told Sujaya: “Excellent!”
Excellent!
You are able to inquire about such a profound meaning from the Tathāgata. Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain and resolve whatever you doubt.
The Deva Most Victorious said, "So be it!"
"I wish to hear it!
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Most Victorious:
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!"
The single dharma that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in, which enables them to penetrate all dharmas, is namely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, they will then be able to penetrate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge.
“O Devaputra!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), become able to penetrate the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)?”
"O Heavenly King,

you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are then able to practice the perfection of the sublime gift of Dharma (dharmadānapāramitā)."

This means that with a pure mind and no expectations, one teaches the Dharma to others without seeking fame or profit, but solely for the sake of extinguishing suffering; one does not perceive a self who can teach the Dharma to them, nor does one perceive those who listen, because there is no duality, no distinction, and because all things are devoid of intrinsic nature.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to practice the perfection of the fearless gift (*abhaya-dāna*).
This means that by regarding sentient beings as one would one's own parents, brothers, or relatives, they cause all beings to feel intimate attachment toward them."

Why is this? Because since beginningless time, all beings have transmigrated through the six realms of existence as our own kinsmen; if we would even risk our own lives to rescue sentient beings from fear and hardship, how much more so should we refrain from inflicting harm or distress upon them!
One does not perceive oneself as being able to bestow fearlessness upon others, nor does one perceive the recipient; for there is no duality, no distinction, and they are devoid of intrinsic nature.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of generosity that provides the necessities of life."

This means that one gives various requisites according to the needs of sentient beings, causing them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action; yet one does not perceive a self that can give those requisites to others, nor does one perceive the recipient, because there is no duality, no distinction, and they are by nature detached.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to practice the perfection of giving that is free from expectation of reward.

This means that when practicing giving, they do not hope for a karmic result; it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for a bodhisattva to give. They do not perceive a self that can practice giving free from reward, nor do they perceive the reward of the gift, because these are non-dual, without distinction, and devoid of intrinsic nature."
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to practice the perfection of giving through great compassion.
That is to say, seeing sentient beings who are impoverished, aged, sick, and without refuge, they give rise to a mind of great compassion and make this vow:

'When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I shall act as a place of refuge for all sentient beings. For the sake of sentient beings, they dedicate even small roots of virtue toward bodhi; yet they do not discriminate between themselves as the savior and others as those to be saved, because there is no duality, no distinction, and their intrinsic nature is detached."
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of respectful giving.

This means that according to whatever items sentient beings require, they promptly offer them with respect without causing weariness; they do not perceive a self who can practice respectful giving, nor do they perceive a recipient, because there is no duality, no distinction, and because their intrinsic nature is detached.”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to practice the *dānapāramitā* of honoring.

This means that toward sentient beings, they give with a mind of respect, conceiving of them as teachers or as parents. If they have no material wealth, they bestow kind words; yet they do not perceive a self who can practice the giving of honor, nor do they perceive a recipient. This is because there is no duality, no distinction, and all things are devoid of intrinsic nature."
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to practice the perfection of giving through offerings.

That is to say, upon seeing a caitya or a monastic residence, they should sweep and sprinkle it, making offerings with various flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth. If they see a sacred image or the True Dharma falling into decay, they should diligently restore and make offerings to it. If they see the monastic community, they should provide them with food, drink, bedding, and medicine. Yet they do not perceive a self that performs the offering, nor do they perceive a recipient; for these are non-dual, without distinction, and devoid of intrinsic nature.”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to practice the perfection of giving without dependence.
This means that when practicing giving, they do not form such thoughts:
'May I, by means of this gift, be reborn among gods or humans, become a king of gods or humans, and enjoy wealth, nobility, and pleasure.'"
"Furthermore, they do not grasp after or seek even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, because nothing is to be apprehended.
O Heavenly King!
This is called the practice and study of the perfection of wisdom by bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through which they are able to penetrate the perfection of giving."
“O Heavenly King!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), become able to penetrate the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)?”
"O Heavenly King,
you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline."
It means that bodhisattvas reflect as follows:

"Within the pure teaching of the Vinaya, the Buddha has spoken the Sūtra on the Precepts corresponding to Prātimokṣa, which a bodhisattva should study. One should not perceive the characteristics of the precepts nor the act of receiving and upholding them; one should not be attached to views regarding the precepts, nor attached to a self, because they are non-dual, without distinction, and devoid of intrinsic nature."
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are then able to practice the *śīlapāramitā*.
This means that bodhisattvas reflect as follows:

‘The unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas is not attained merely by upholding pure ethical discipline; rather, one must train extensively in all the bodhisattva precepts and practices. For the nature of the precepts is cool and tranquil, non-arising, non-dual, undifferentiated, and by nature detached.’”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
This means that bodhisattvas reflect as follows:
'How can the observance of precepts sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)?'"
The afflictions are of three kinds: greed, hatred, and delusion; each of these is further divided into three—superior, middling, and inferior.
One should know the remedies for severing these afflictions:
for one in whom greed predominates, one should cultivate the contemplation of impurity, fully observing the thirty-six components of the body.
Those for whom hatred predominates should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion;
those for whom delusion predominates should cultivate the contemplation of dependent origination.
This is because one does not perceive a subject that contemplates nor an object that is contemplated, as they are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
This means that bodhisattvas reflect as follows:
‘How should a bodhisattva correctly distance themselves from improper reflection?’”
That is to say, bodhisattvas do not give rise to such thoughts as:
"I practice the path of tranquility, the path of detachment, and the path of emptiness, whereas all other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas dwell in clamor and do not delight in the practice of emptiness."
"By seeing that there is no duality and knowing that self-nature is free from [conceptualization], one is then able to distance oneself from improper mental attention.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they will then be able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline."

This means that although Bodhisattvas know all phenomena to be empty and detached, they deeply fear all transgressions. As the Buddha has taught, they should maintain pure precepts, cultivate various meritorious deeds up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and harbor great dread even toward minor offenses, refusing to cohabit with them; for the World-Honored One said:
"For example, whether a dose of poison is large or small, both are harmful."
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline.

This means that bodhisattvas always give rise to a sense of dread and remain in accord with faithful practice; even when staying alone in a secluded place without a companion, if there were śramaṇas or others who brought gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, and other such jewels to entrust to the bodhisattva, they would not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment or desire to take them, but would reflect thus:
'The World-Honored One has constantly said:'"
"It would be better to cut off one's own flesh and eat it than to take the wealth of others when it has not been given.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline.

This refers to bodhisattvas whose observance of the precepts is firm; even if Māra or his retinues attempt to test them by assuming exquisite forms and appearances, the bodhisattva’s mind remains unshaken, reflecting:

"The World-Honored One has constantly taught that all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are like dreams, illusions, and transformations—non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature."
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are then able to practice the *śīlapāramitā*.

This means that although these bodhisattvas diligently uphold the precepts, they do not long for the status of a human or celestial king; their bodies are free from the three faults, their speech is devoid of the four errors, and their minds are exempt from the three transgressions. Upholding the precepts in this way, they do not perceive a self who upholds them, nor do they perceive the characteristics of the precepts; it is non-dual and undifferentiated, because its intrinsic nature is detached.”
“O Devaputra!
This is called the training in the perfection of wisdom by which bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to penetrate the perfection of ethical discipline.”
“O Heavenly King!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by practicing and training in the perfection of wisdom, become able to penetrate the perfection of patience?”
"O Heavenly King,
you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of patience."

This means that bodhisattvas constantly train in internal patience (*adhyātma-kṣānti*), such that they are not followed by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction; they also train in external patience (*bahirdhā-kṣānti*), never giving rise to anger even when others strike, revile, deceive, rob, or humiliate them; and they also train in the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*). As the World-Honored One has taught—that the profound true nature is the absence of phenomena, the absence of self, the absence of arising, and quiescence, which is itself nirvāṇa—they are not terrified upon hearing such a teaching. They reflect thus:

"If I do not train in this Dharma, how could I attain the sought-after unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and how could I bring benefit and peace to all classes of sentient beings until the end of the future?"
He reflected with careful discernment upon the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion: "In what place does each of these arise?
By what causes and conditions are they produced?
By what causes and conditions are they extinguished?"

Observing reality as it is, one perceives neither a producer nor a produced, neither a destroyer nor a destroyed. Thus, the mind of patience continues in an uninterrupted succession, remaining constant day and night without any interval. Regarding the objects of patience, there is no discriminative thought, such as thinking, "I should practice patience toward kings, parents, and teachers, but I may treat others with malice."

When a bodhisattva practices patience, it is not for the sake of seeking recompense, fame, profit, benevolence, righteousness, fear, or shame; rather, it is because the nature of a bodhisattva is such that they ought to practice patience.
Thus, even if others inflict harm, beat them, revile them, plunder from them, or treat them with contempt, their mind remains unshaken.

If a bodhisattva occupies a position such as that of a king or a minister and is reviled, insulted, or humiliated by a person of low station or poverty, they shall never act with sudden violence or abruptly display punitive force, thinking, "I dwell in a position of honor and thus it is appropriate for me to reprimand and punish.
Instead, they should reflect: "In the presence of the World-Honored Buddhas of the past, I made a great vow:
'I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings and cause them to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. If I were now to give rise to anger, I would violate my original vow."
It is like a skilled physician who makes this vow:
"I shall treat all those in the world who suffer from cataracts; if I myself lose my sight, how could I cure the ailments of others?
In the same way, how can a bodhisattva who gives rise to anger within themselves ever be able to rescue others from their darkness?
"One does not perceive a self that can endure, nor an object that is endured; for these are non-dual, without distinction, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
O Heavenly King!
This is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through which they are able to penetrate the perfection of patience."
“O Devaputra!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom, become able to penetrate the perfection of diligence?”
"O Heavenly King,
you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are thereby able to practice the perfection of diligence."

This means that when bodhisattvas cause those who have not yet extinguished [afflictions] to extinguish them, those who have not yet crossed over to cross over, those who have not yet been liberated to be liberated, those who have not yet been established in peace to be established in peace, and those who have not yet awakened to awaken—while the bodhisattvas are thus practicing diligence, various evil Māras create obstacles for them and say to the bodhisattva:
"O son of good family!..."
Do not practice this path and undergo toil and suffering in vain. Why is this?
In the past, I practiced this very path;

yet it did not cause those who had not extinguished [afflictions] to extinguish them, nor those who had not crossed over to cross over, nor those who had not been liberated to be liberated, nor those who had not been established in peace to be established in peace, nor those who had not awakened to awaken—thus I underwent toil and suffering in vain, with no real benefit at all.

"Since long ago, I have seen many bodhisattvas who practiced and studied this path but all eventually regressed; you should turn your mind toward the path of the two vehicles, attain the fruits of those two vehicles, and achieve your own nirvāṇa."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva immediately recognized it and said to the evil Māra:

"Go back on your way! My mind is as firm and solid as a diamond; it cannot be shaken or destroyed by your deceptive words. By persisting in your attempts to obstruct me, you will only bring suffering upon yourself for a long night."
Upon hearing these words, Māra vanished and was no longer seen.

If other bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the *prajñāpāramitā* were to practice the first five *pāramitās* for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they would still be able to surpass them when a bodhisattva practices such diligence; how much more so, then, the stages of the two vehicles!

Thus, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they accomplish the Buddha-dharmas and remain free from all evils. Although they practice diligence that is neither too swift nor too slow, they are able to give rise to this sublime great vow:

"May my body become equal to that of the Tathāgata, with the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of my head and the white *ūrṇā* hair-tuft between my eyebrows; as the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, may I do likewise."
"Just as pure gold becomes magnificent and pure when polished and adorned with various jewels, so too is the vigor of a bodhisattva:

it is free from all defilements—namely, laziness, indolence, exhaustion, lack of self-awareness, and improper reflection. By means of this, one is able to attain superior, pure merit and wisdom with which one is adorned; the body does not grow weary and the mind is free from weariness or sloth. All obstructive, evil, and unwholesome dharmas are caused to be eliminated, and all factors conducive to the path that lead toward nirvana are made to increase.
Even minor evils do not arise, let alone those that are numerous!"

Even if the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were filled with great fires like those of the Avīci Hell, a Bodhisattva would still pass through them for the sake of even a single sentient being who could be liberated beyond this world, let alone for many!
These bodhisattvas do not harbor such thoughts as:

"Unsurpassed enlightenment is not easily attained; the bodhisattva’s cultivation is like one whose head is on fire, requiring the passage of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas—such a heavy burden is truly difficult to bear."
One should simply reflect thus:

"All Buddhas of the past and present cultivated this practice to realize great enlightenment; I too must likewise cultivate it correctly. Rather than entering nirvana swiftly, I would prefer to remain in the hells for hundreds of thousands of eons so that all sentient beings may attain liberation."

When a bodhisattva practices diligence in this manner, the mind does not exalt itself nor disparage others; they do not perceive an agent who practices nor the phenomena being practiced, for these are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
“O Devaputra!
This is called the practice and training in the perfection of wisdom by which bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to penetrate the perfection of diligence.”
“O Devaputra!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom, become able to penetrate the perfection of meditative concentration?”
"O Heavenly King,
you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to practice the perfection of meditative concentration."

It refers to those bodhisattvas who have deeply planted roots of goodness within the Mahāyāna, who throughout successive lifetimes have extensively cultivated sublime conduct and drawn near to virtuous friends; who are never born into families of poverty, low status, or wrong views, but always take birth among the great clans of brahmins or kṣatriyas; who possess right faith in the Triple Gem and cause wholesome dharmas to increase; and who, by virtue of their past roots of goodness, form this thought:
"Sentient beings wander through the various realms for a long night, and the wheel of suffering turns without ceasing solely because of craving."
Having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva gave rise to a mind of weary detachment, knowing that [desire] exists only through false conceptualization:

"In the sūtras, the World-Honored One has taught through various skillful means that the faults of desire are like spears, like javelins, like swords, like snakes, like bubbles, and like foam—foul, impure, subject to transformation, and impermanent. How could a wise person be greedily attached to such things?"

He immediately shaved off his hair and beard, left the household life, and practiced the Way. Regarding what he had not yet seen, he claimed to see it; regarding what he had not yet attained, he claimed to have attained it; regarding what he had not yet realized, he claimed to have realized it. Upon hearing the teachings—whether they pertained to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) or ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—he accepted and upheld them, practicing according to reality and observing in accordance with the Dharma. That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. He remained far removed from clamor and distraction, did not seek fame or reputation, nor did he seek offerings or honor. With body and mind full of vigor, he was never weary or idle, reflecting: "In what objects does this mind mostly dwell?"
Is it for the sake of the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate?

If one encounters an unwholesome object, one should immediately cease [the engagement]; if one encounters an indeterminate object, one should likewise abandon it; but if one encounters a wholesome object, one should apply diligent effort to encourage the growth of superior roots of goodness.
In order to counteract unwholesome and evil states, the thirty-seven sublime factors of enlightenment are brought forth.
These unwholesome and evil states refer to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Greed, moreover, is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior.

Those of superior-grade greed, upon hearing the names of sensual objects, leap with their entire bodies and rejoice from the depths of their hearts; they do not contemplate the faults of desire, no sense of weary detachment arises, they pursue them through improper means, and they lack shame and remorse.

Regarding those without shame and remorse: when walking alone, they constantly think of sensual objects wherever they travel; their minds follow one another in succession without ever momentarily abandoning them; seeing only what is exquisite and beautiful, they do not recognize its dangers. When parents, teachers, or elders rebuke their desires, they feel no shame or embarrassment and fail to realize that a dispute has arisen.

Such individuals are called those without shame and remorse; at the end of their lives, this class of people shall fall into the evil realms. Those of middle-grade greed do not give rise to lustful thoughts when separated from sensual objects.
Those with inferior-grade greed have their lustful passions extinguished merely through conversation and laughter.
Hatred also has three grades:

those with superior-grade hatred, when their fury erupts, become mentally bewildered and vision-disordered; they may commit an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, or slander the True Dharma, or further commit other grave karmic offenses many hundreds of thousands of times greater than the five *ānantarya* sins.
Those with medium-grade anger, due to their state of malice, immediately give rise to remorse even as they commit various evils;
those with low-grade anger harbor no resentment in their hearts, but feel regret as soon as they utter words of reproach or slander.
Ignorance (*moha*) likewise has three grades, which should be understood according to reason.

Although one performs this contemplation, one knows that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, reflections, shadows, mirages, transformations, and cities of the *gandharvas*, because they are false, unreal, and inverted. Thus, seeing the cessation of external objects, the internal mind becomes tranquil; one no longer perceives the agent of action or the phenomena acted upon, for they are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
“O Devaputra!
This is called the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, which enables them to penetrate the Dhyānapāramitā.”
“O Devaputra!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom so that they are able to penetrate the perfection of wisdom?”
"O Heavenly King,
you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are then able to practice the perfection of wisdom."

This means that when Bodhisattvas contemplate form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness with correct wisdom, they do not perceive the arising of form, they do not perceive the accumulation of form, and they do not perceive the cessation of form; it is likewise for feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is entirely empty and lacks any reality; there are only provisional designations of names. While practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* to transform all sentient beings, one never speaks of the non-existence of karma or its results.

Although they know that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, reflections, shadows, mirages, transformations, and cities of Gandharvas—devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, or a pudgala—they nonetheless constantly proclaim that there is karma and its fruit.
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, the retinues of Māra cannot find an opportunity to harm them. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattvas associate with virtuous friends and accomplish the world-transcending factors that assist awakening; they joyfully praise the profound, true Dharma of all Tathāgatas. Among all devas, māras, brahmās, and other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, none can equal them except for the Buddha’s own right knowledge. They do not perceive an agent who acts nor the phenomena that are acted upon, because these are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
“O Devaputra!
This is called the training in the perfection of wisdom by the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through which they are able to penetrate the perfection of wisdom.”
“O Heavenly King!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom, become able to penetrate the perfection of skillful means?”
"O Heavenly King,

you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are then able to practice the perfection of skillful means (upāyakauśalyapāramitā)."

It refers to the skillful means of bodhisattvas who dedicate [their merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Whenever they see superior and exquisite flowers or fruits in the world, they constantly offer them to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, never failing for even a moment throughout the six periods of day and night; they dedicate these supreme virtues toward enlightenment. They do the same whenever they see trees bearing flowers or fruit.

If one hears the profound meaning of the Dharma taught within the Tathāgata’s sūtras, receives it with joy and faith, delights in reciting and upholding it, and explains it to others, dedicating this sublime merit toward Bodhi.

If one sees the form or image of a Tathāgata stūpa, one should immediately offer various kinds of incense and flowers, vowing that all sentient beings may be free from the scent of broken precepts and attain the fragrance of pure morality like that of the Buddhas;
by sweeping, sprinkling, and smearing the ground, one vows that all sentient beings may have their dignified deportment perfectly composed;
by covering it with flower canopies, one vows that all sentient beings may be entirely freed from the heat of affliction.
Upon entering a monastic dwelling, he made the vow: "May all sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon leaving a monastic dwelling, he made the vow: "May all sentient beings emerge from the realm of Māra.
Seeing the monastery gate being opened, he then made this vow:
"By means of supramundane wisdom, I shall open for all sentient beings the gates that have not yet been opened, causing them all to awaken and enter [the path].
If I see them closed, may I close the three realms of existence or the four evil destinies for the sake of sentient beings;
if I attain a peaceful seat, may all sentient beings sit upon the seat of enlightenment.
When lying on my right side, may all sentient beings realize parinirvāṇa;
when rising from sitting or lying down, may all sentient beings be free from all arising afflictions;
and when washing my feet, may all sentient beings be far removed from dust and defilement.
When he pays homage to the Buddha and circumambulates the stūpa, he makes the vow that all sentient beings shall become Buddhas; yet he does not feel joy when gods and humans pay him respect.
If there are followers of external paths with wrong views who are difficult to transform, he thinks to himself:
"I am their teacher, but because they are possessed by pride, they will certainly not believe me; for now, I shall act as their fellow student or even their disciple."

Although he dwelt among that multitude, his observance of the precepts and his great learning surpassed those of all non-Buddhists; consequently, they were subdued and honored him as their teacher, accepting his words with faith. He refuted their false doctrines and expounded the true Nirvana, leading them into the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-teachings. Therein they diligently cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and samādhi, attaining superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and extensively practicing sublime virtues.

Seeing those with excessive desire, he transforms himself into a woman of supreme beauty to cause them to become attached; in an instant, he manifests her impermanence—her complexion changing, her body bloating, rotting, and emitting a foul odor—causing them to feel deep loathing and give rise to a mind of weary detachment. He then immediately returns to his original form as a bodhisattva and, for their sake, expounds the essential points of the profound Dharma, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so that they may practice the Mahāyāna and achieve the unsurpassed fruit.

Seeing those who follow the Mahāyāna but have become separated from virtuous friends, such that although they apply themselves with diligence to study the path of the two vehicles, they are unable to realize its fruit and thus lose the benefit of the unsurpassed Dharma of the Mahāyāna;

he observes their faculties and preaches the Mahāyāna for them, causing them to turn their minds toward the unsurpassed path. For those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, he transforms them so that they may resolve to do so; for those who have already resolved, he encourages them to remain steadfast.
Seeing a person who upholds the precepts commit a minor, light offense, yet fail to confess and repent, becoming indolent, discouraged, and sorrowful— thereby unable to advance in the sublime path—
he explains the Dharma for them so that they may quickly repent and eliminate the fault, their minds freed from sorrow and anxiety as they advance in the sublime path.

This assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, possessing few desires and being content, seeks exclusively the benefit of the Dharma and preaches it for the sake of sentient beings as an offering to the Tathāgata; by means of this, they accomplish the six pāramitās:
preaching the Dharma as an offering constitutes the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā);
acting without contradicting one’s words constitutes the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
That gods, Māras, and others cannot disrupt or disturb it is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
that the succession of moments of mind does not perceive weariness or fatigue is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
and that one focuses the mind on a single thought-moment without attending to other objects is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
To preach the Dharma as an offering while remaining free from "I" and "mine" is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
This is because one does not perceive an agent who practices nor the dharmas that are practiced; they are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
“O Devaputra!
This is called the training in the perfection of wisdom by bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which enables them to penetrate the perfection of skillful means.”
“O Heavenly King!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), become able to penetrate the perfection of sublime vows (praṇidhānapāramitā)?”
"O Heavenly King,
you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are then able to practice the perfection of sublime vows (praṇidhānapāramitā)."

This means that whatever aspirations these bodhisattvas may have, they do not seek the pleasures experienced by worldly beings, nor do they seek for themselves the escape from the three realms or the bliss of nirvana attained by practicing the paths of the two vehicles; rather, they make this aspiration:
"May all sentient beings enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, and only then shall my own body finally attain perfect enlightenment."

Those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment are transformed so that they may resolve; those who have already resolved are led to cultivate the Great Practice; those who have cultivated the Great Practice are led to attain Bodhi; and those who have attained Bodhi are exhorted to preach the Dharma. This process continues successively until after their parinirvāṇa, when stūpas are erected of the seven precious jewels to enshrine their śarīra, and offerings are made so that immeasurable multitudes may obtain boundless merit.
He further made this vow:
"In all worlds where Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment, may there be no interference or disturbance from celestial Māras or various non-Buddhist paths;
may I, through my own wisdom, give rise to the unsurpassed mind, not relying on external conditions, so that once it has arisen, I shall never regress."
Furthermore, I vow that I shall always remain in the world to bring sentient beings to maturity and cause them to obtain benefit and happiness;
I vow that when bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds hear the Tathāgata teach the profound Dharma, they will realize it as it truly is and their hearts will be free from fear;

and I vow that all sentient beings may attain great wisdom, thoroughly penetrating the boundless path of the Buddhas, the boundless realm of the Buddhas, and boundless great compassion, thereby benefiting infinite classes of sentient beings.
These bodhisattvas mostly aspire for themselves to always dwell in defiled lands and not be born in pure lands.
Why is this? It is because one who has an illness relies upon medicine and a physician; if there were no illness, medicine and a physician would be of no use.
When a bodhisattva makes such sublime vows, they do not perceive a subject that practices nor an object of practice, for these are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
"O Heavenly King!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ cultivation and study of the *prajñāpāramitā*, by which they are able to penetrate the *praṇidhānapāramitā*.
“O Devaputra!
"How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), become able to penetrate the perfection of power (balapāramitā)?
O Heavenly King, you should know this!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are then able to practice the *balapāramitā*.

This means that because these bodhisattvas have subdued the Māras and demons and crushed all non-Buddhists, and are fully endowed with the power of merit and wisdom, there are no Buddha-dharmas they do not cultivate, and there are no Buddha-realms they do not realize and perceive.

By means of supernormal powers, they can lift Jambudvīpa, or the four continents, or a great trichiliocosm, or even worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers throughout the ten directions with the tip of a single hair, and place them back in their original locations without causing any harm;
or by means of spiritual power, they can take various kinds of jewels from the midst of space and bestow them upon sentient beings;
and they are able to hear and retain all the teachings of the Buddhas preaching the Dharma throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions.
"One does not perceive the agent of practice nor the phenomena that are practiced, for they are non-dual, without distinction, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
'O Heavenly King!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ cultivation and study of the *prajñāpāramitā*, by which they are able to penetrate the *balapāramitā*."
“O Heavenly King!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), become able to penetrate the perfection of knowledge (jñānapāramitā)?”
"O Devaputra, you should know this!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to practice the *jñānapāramitā*.

This means that all bodhisattvas observe that the arising of the five aggregates is not a real arising, and their cessation is not a real cessation; they contemplate that the five aggregates are ultimately empty, devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a soul, a nourisher, a person, or a pudgala."
Fools, through their inverted and false attachments, do not know as it truly is that the aggregates are not the self and that there is no self within the aggregates;

nor do they know as it truly is that the self is not the aggregates and that there are no aggregates within the self. Consequently, they wander through the cycle of birth and death in the various realms of existence, like a whirling firebrand, through the deluded attachments of fools.

However, all phenomena are by nature originally empty, without arising and without ceasing. When conditions combine, we speak of arising; when conditions disperse, we speak of ceasing. In reality, there is no arising or ceasing. Because their nature is not non-existent, one cannot say they arise; because their nature is not existent, one cannot say they cease.

These bodhisattvas have no single phenomenon among all objects that they do not thoroughly penetrate. By practicing this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they cannot be obscured by those of the two vehicles or by non-Buddhists; observing with wisdom, they are completely clear and lucid from the first generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) until their final nirvāṇa.
They are able to know all objects through a single phenomenon, and they realize that all objects are not separate from that single phenomenon.
Why is this so? Because it is suchness (*tathatā*).

When these bodhisattvas cultivate this wisdom, they do not perceive a cultivator or that which is cultivated, for there is no duality, no distinction, and they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
“O Heavenly King!

This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ cultivation and study of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by which they are able to penetrate the perfection of knowledge (jñānapāramitā). This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation and study of a single dharma, by which they are able to penetrate all dharmas.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 566; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 567.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter 3: Revealing Characteristics (Lakṣaṇasaṃdarśana), Part Six. At that time, the Most Victorious One rose again from his seat, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What are the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said to Ajita:
“Great King, you should know this!”
"Just as the characteristics of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Varaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has characteristics like those of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth?
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!"
Pervasive, vast, and difficult to measure—this is the characteristic of the earth; so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this?
Because the suchness of all phenomena is universal, vast, and difficult to measure.
O Heavenly King, you should know that all medicinal herbs grow depending upon the earth;
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this, for it is universally able to produce and grow all wholesome dharmas.

O Heavenly King, you should know that it is just as the great earth feels no joy when increased and no sorrow when diminished, because it is free from "I" and "mine," being devoid of dualistic characteristics.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise: it does not increase through praise nor decrease through disparagement, for it is free from "I" and "mine," being devoid of dualistic characteristics.
Furthermore, just as the great earth is that upon which all those who come and go in the world rely when lifting or setting down their feet;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, for there is no one seeking a happy rebirth or proceeding toward *nirvāṇa* who does not rely upon it.
Furthermore, just as the great earth produces various kinds of jewels, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: it gives birth to all the various merits of the world.
Furthermore, just as the great earth cannot be shaken by various afflictions such as insects, ants, mosquitoes, or gadflies, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*:
being free from "I" and "mine," it is entirely devoid of conceptual discrimination and cannot be shaken.
Furthermore, just as the great earth is never startled or terrified upon hearing the sounds of lions, dragons, elephants, and the like;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which no celestial Māras or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) can frighten.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a self, nor does one perceive phenomena, for their intrinsic nature is empty.
"O Devaputra, you should know this!"
Just as the element of water flows from high to low, serving as the refuge for all aquatic life;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: flowing from the true *dharmadhātu* toward the world, it is the basis upon which all wholesome dharmas rely.
Furthermore, just as the element of water can moisten grasses and trees, causing them to produce flowers and fruit;

so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: it moistens all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), giving rise to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), accomplishing omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and attaining the fruit of the Buddha-dharmas, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, just as the element of water, when it saturates the roots of grasses and trees, can cause them to be uprooted and carried away by the current;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, for it can extinguish the roots of all views, inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies, such that they never arise again.
Furthermore, just as the element of water is by nature fundamentally pure, stainless, and unclouded;

so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: its essence is free from afflictions and is thus called "pure"; it is able to distance one from all delusions and is thus called "stainless"; and because it is of a single characteristic and not diverse, it is called "unclouded."
Just as a person suffering from the heat of summer finds refreshing coolness upon encountering water,
so too shall sentient beings tormented by the heat of affliction who hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* necessarily attain coolness and be freed from all such torments.
Just as a person suffering from thirst finds relief only upon obtaining water;
so too, one seeking the supramundane Dharma finds satisfaction through the attainment of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the fulfillment of one's aspirations.
Furthermore, just as a spring or pond is extremely deep and difficult to enter, so too is this *prajñāpāramitā*, the realm of all Buddhas, profoundly deep and difficult to enter.
Furthermore, just as water is level in all places, even in pits and hollows;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is entirely equal toward all *pratyekabuddhas*, *śrāvakas*, and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, just as pure water washes away filth and impurities to bring about clarity and purity, so too does a bodhisattva, by penetrating the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and becoming free from all afflictions (kleśa), attain purity.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is pure by nature, being free from all delusions.
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!"
For example, although the element of fire burns all trees, medicinal herbs, and grasses, it does not think,
"I am able to burn things. In the same way,
although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can forever extinguish all afflictions and their habitual tendencies, it does not think:
"I am able to extinguish [them] forever.
Furthermore, just as the fire element is able to fully ripen all categories of things, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; it is likewise able to ripen all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, just as the fire element can completely dry up all moist things, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*:
it can completely dry up all the floods of the outflows (*āsrava*) so that they never arise again.

Furthermore, it is like a mass of fire atop the Snowy Mountains: although it can illuminate from afar for one yojana, even up to ten yojanas, it has no such thought as, "I am able to illuminate the distant."
The profound perfection of wisdom is likewise: although it illuminates the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, it does not think, "I am able to illuminate them."

"Furthermore, just as birds and beasts see a fire at night and, out of fear, flee far away, so too do ordinary beings of meager merit, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas feel dread upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā and abandon it."
It is difficult even to hear the name of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, let alone to practice and study it! It is like one traveling far at night who has lost the right path;

if they see the light of a fire, they feel great joy, knowing there is a village nearby, and they hasten toward it. Upon reaching it, they find peace and security, forever free from fear. Likewise, in the vast night of birth and death, those with merit who hear the *prajñāpāramitā* will feel great joy; by upholding, reciting, and studying it, they will forever leave behind the afflictions and their minds will attain peace and happiness.
Just as fire in the world is the same for both the noble and the lowly, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*:

it is equally present in both noble beings (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Just as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas all make offerings to fire, so do all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all make offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, just as a small fire can burn a trichiliocosm, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*:
if one hears even a single phrase, it can incinerate immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*).
“O Deva-king, you should know!
Just as the element of wind can cause all types of things to grow, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: it can cause all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas to grow.”
Furthermore, just as when the element of wind increases in intensity, it is able to universally destroy and obliterate all categories of things;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: if its cultivation increases in intensity, it can universally destroy and obliterate the afflictions of birth and death.
Furthermore, just as the element of wind can cause all that is stiflingly hot to become cool and refreshing, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*:
it enables sentient beings who are stifled by the heat of afflictions to realize the cool, eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, just as the element of wind blows and drifts without ceasing, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: it abides nowhere at all among all phenomena.

"O Heavenly King, you should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is stainless, unattached, tranquil, immeasurable, and boundless wisdom. It penetrates the true nature of all phenomena with equanimity; like the nature of great empty space, it has no place of abiding, is free from the marks of objective spheres, and transcends discursive thought and investigation. Mind and mental factors are entirely without discrimination, without arising, and without cessation, because their intrinsic nature is detached."
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings in a manner as rare in this world as the sun and moon are for all enjoyments."
Just as the cool moon can dispel the heat of affliction, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: it can eliminate the feverish poison of all afflictions.
Furthermore, just as the bright moon is a joy for all to behold in the world,
so too is the profound Prajñāpāramitā a joy for all noble and holy ones to behold.

Furthermore, just as the white moon waxes day by day, so too do the bodhisattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom gradually increase from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until they realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.

Furthermore, just as the moon in the dark fortnight diminishes day by day until it is completely gone, so too do the afflictions and latent tendencies of the bodhisattvas gradually diminish and vanish as they practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, just as the full moon is praised by all Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others, so too are those sons and daughters of good family who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* praised by the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.

Furthermore, just as the moon travels throughout the realms of the four continents, so too is it with the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); there is no place among form, mind, and so forth that it does not pervade.
Furthermore, just as the pure moon is always naturally adorned, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: its nature is fundamentally pure and it is eternally self-adorned.
Why is this? Because its fundamental nature is free from defilement, unarisen, and unceasing, pervading all phenomena, for its self-nature is inherently detached.
It is like the blazing sun, which, though it dispels all darkness, does not think to itself:
"I am able to destroy them.
In the same way, although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* destroys all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) from beginningless time, it does not think:
"I am able to destroy them."
"Furthermore, just as the scorching sun, though it causes the lotuses to bloom, does not think,
'I am able to open them,' so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: though it opens the minds of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it does not think:"
"I am able to open them.
Furthermore, it is like the brilliant sun: although it illuminates the ten directions, it does not think or say, "I am able to illuminate everywhere."
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise: although it illuminates the boundless, it possesses no mark of illumination.

Just as when one sees the sign of crimson light appearing in the eastern quarter, one knows that the solar disc will soon emerge; so too, if one hears the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that this person is not far from the Buddha.

Just as the virtuous men and women of Jambudvīpa experience great joy upon seeing the rising of the sun, so too do all the noble ones feel immense delight when the name of the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.

Furthermore, just as when the sun rises, the moon and the stars all cease to appear, so too when Bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the merits of the non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles cease to appear.

Furthermore, just as one can only see the depressions and elevations of the terrain when the sun rises, so too, when Bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the world then comes to know the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is equal in its own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), being without arising or cessation, and by nature detached.
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they extensively cultivate the practice of emptiness without dwelling or attachment; they cultivate the path of illumination to eliminate the obscurations of darkness; they distance themselves from evil associates and draw near to all Buddhas; their minds succeed one another in continuous mindfulness of the Buddha without interruption; and they penetrate equality, accord with the *dharmadhātu*.
Although they sport with supernatural powers throughout the lands of the ten directions, their bodies remain in their original lands without ever wavering.
They contemplate the teachings of all Buddhas as if seeing them directly before their eyes.
Although they dwell in the world, they are unstained by worldly dharmas, like lotuses that grow from within the mud.
Thus, although a bodhisattva dwells within birth and death, by virtue of the skillful means of profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they remain unstained and unattached. Why is this?
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without arising and without cessation; it is equal in its own characteristics, unseen and unattached, because its nature is utterly secluded.

Furthermore, just as a lotus flower does not retain even a drop of water, so too a bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not allow even the slightest evil to abide for even a moment.

Furthermore, just as a lotus flower emits a fragrant scent wherever it is located, so too does a bodhisattva who practices the profound perfection of wisdom possess the fragrance of ethical discipline throughout cities and villages, whether dwelling among humans or in the heavens.

Furthermore, just as the lotus is pure by nature and is cherished and revered by all, including brahmins, so too the bodhisattva who practices the profound perfection of wisdom is loved and honored by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, other bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.

Furthermore, just as a lotus flower, when first about to bloom, can delight the hearts of all, so too does a bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* smile and speak first, remaining free from frowning, thereby causing all beings to rejoice.

Furthermore, just as seeing a lotus flower is an auspicious sign, so too is seeing it in a dream; for all humans, devas, and others, even hearing or seeing a bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* within a dream is an auspicious omen, let alone hearing or seeing it in reality!

Furthermore, just as a lotus flower in its initial stage of growth is cherished and protected by humans, non-humans, and others alike, so too is a bodhisattva who has first begun to study the perfection of wisdom guarded and protected by all buddhas, bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the gods.
“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they give rise to this thought: ‘I shall, in accordance with reality,
thoroughly penetrate all *pāramitās* and, by teaching and transforming sentient beings, bring the Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment.’”

Seated beneath the Bodhi tree upon the Vajra-seat, he realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma, which possesses twelve kinds of subtle and wondrous characteristics—a wheel that cannot be turned by any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Śakras, or Brahmās in the world;
he transformed and delivered all sentient beings throughout the infinite, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, equally rescuing them from the ocean of birth and death;
he established them in the Prajñāpāramitā, acting as a refuge for those without refuge and a protector for those without protection, and enabling those who wish to see the Buddha to behold him.
They let out the lion’s roar and sported with supernatural powers, extolling the Buddha’s merits to inspire longing and veneration in the assembly;

their minds were pure and never wavered, their intentions were free from flattery or crookedness, and they remained far removed from perverse thoughts—namely, they did not dwell upon the teachings of the two vehicles;
having exhausted all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they were no longer subject to afflictions.
In body, one is free from hypocritical conduct and departs from improper demeanor;
in speech, one is free from deceitful words and speaks according to reality;
receiving kindness, one is always grateful, repaying even small favors with great weight.
The mind harbors no resentment, and the mouth always utters gentle words.
Thus cultivating a pure mind, one perceives neither the defiler nor the defiled phenomena, for they are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
"O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they have faith and understanding in the three kinds of purity of the Tathāgata."
It refers to when bodhisattvas reflect as follows:

"The sūtras state that the body of the Tathāgata is pure—namely, the Dharma-body, the most tranquil body, the unequaled body, the immeasurable body, the unique body, and the vajra-body—and regarding this, my mind is certain and free from doubt."
This is called having faith and understanding that the Tathāgata’s body is pure.
Furthermore, one reflects:

"The sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s speech is pure; thus, he bestows the prediction of buddhahood upon ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and likewise bestows the prediction of buddhahood upon bodhisattvas. One should have faith that such words are logically consistent and not contradictory."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is forever free from all faults, has exhausted all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and is without further afflictions; he is tranquil and pure.
It is impossible for anyone—whether gods, Māras, Brahmās, or any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—to find any failure in the Tathāgata’s verbal karma.
This is called the purity of faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words.
Furthermore, one reflects:

"The sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s intention is pure; regarding the dharmas contemplated by the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, no one—whether śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, devas, humans, or other sentient beings—is able to know them."

Why is this? Because the mind of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and difficult to enter; it is free from all discursive thought and investigation, beyond the realm of deliberation, immeasurable and boundless like the realm of empty space. One who believes and understands this with such a mind will have no doubt.
This is called "faithful understanding through the purity of the Tathāgata’s intention.
O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect in this way:

"As the Buddha has taught, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shoulder the heavy burden for the sake of all sentient beings; they are firm and without retreat, neither terrified nor weary, as they practice in succession the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge. They accomplish the Buddha-dharmas—unobstructed, unimpeded, boundless, incomparable, and unique qualities;
their speech is definitive, their nature is courageous, and they accomplish the vast and great deeds of a Tathāgata."
"In these matters, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are without confusion or doubt, and they accept them with profound faith in their hearts.
O Heavenly King, you should know this!"
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect as follows:

"As the Buddha has taught, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and ultimately sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they are able to attain the unimpeded and pure supernormal powers of the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. In a single moment, through the power of equalizing wisdom, they penetrate the three periods of time and observe all worlds as they truly are: 'There are sentient beings who possess evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind; they revile the noble ones and, due to wrong views, perform wrong actions. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall fall into the evil destinies.'"

In this way, sentient beings who possess excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind, who praise the noble ones, and who perform right actions based on right view, will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a happy destination.
Having observed the realm of sentient beings as it truly is, one reflects:
"In the past, I made the vow to practice the bodhisattva path to awaken myself and to awaken others; this vow should now be fulfilled."
"In these matters, those bodhisattvas are without confusion or doubt, accepting them with faith as they truly are.

O Heavenly King, you should know that the place where all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain Buddhahood is called the 'site of awakening' (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because they are able to awaken themselves, they are called 'Perfectly Awakened Ones' (*samyaksaṃbuddha*); because they are able to awaken sentient beings, they are called 'Universally Perfectly Awakened Ones' (*samyaksaṃbuddha*)."
"O Heavenly King, you should know that these bodhisattvas,
practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, have faith and understanding that the Tathāgata appears in the world to benefit, bring peace, and bring happiness to all sentient beings."

"O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to hear the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and accept it with deep faith."

Why is this? That which is spoken by all Buddhas is true and not false; all various other vehicles emerge from the Buddha-vehicle.
