*vipaśyanā* means seeing dharmas as they truly are, and *śamatha* means the single-mindedness of not being distracted.

When a bodhisattva has thus cultivated the practice of contemplation, they immediately attain pure precepts; because the precepts are pure, their conduct is also pure. This is called the bodhisattva’s pure practice of contemplating the profound perfection of wisdom.
“O Heavenly King, you should know!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they uphold the unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata and listen to and receive the true Dharma. For the sake of protecting the Dharma, they do not seek gain or offerings;
for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed, they do not seek honor.”
It is for the sake of guarding and protecting the practice of the Mahāyāna, and not for the sake of fame or reputation;
it is so that those without refuge may find refuge, those without protection may find protection, those without peace may find peace, and those without the eye of wisdom may obtain the eye of wisdom;

it is to show the path of the Śrāvaka to those who cultivate the Hīnayāna, to show the path of the Pratyekabuddha to those who study the Madhyamāyāna, and to show the Unsurpassed Path to those who practice the Mahāyāna—thus listening to the Dharma for the sake of unsurpassed wisdom, and never for the sake of attaining an inferior vehicle.

“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they skillfully understand the various *vinaya* dharmas— namely, the *vinaya*, the practice of the *vinaya*, the profundity of the *vinaya*, the subtlety of the *vinaya*, the pure and the impure, the faulty and the faultless, the root of the *Prātimokṣa*, the *vinaya* of the Śrāvakas, and the *vinaya* of the Bodhisattvas.”
"These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are thoroughly proficient in all such rules of discipline (*vinaya*).
O Heavenly King, you should know this!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they skillfully understand all modes of conduct and ethical discipline, and they skillfully train in the precepts undertaken by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

Having cultivated the practice of the precepts, if one observes that another’s deportment does not accord with the expectations of the assembly, one should distance oneself from them and refrain from acting in such improper places;
if there is a śramaṇa whose deportment and practice of the precepts are complete, pure, and stainless, one should draw near to them;
if there are brāhmaṇas or followers of other paths engaged in different practices, one should encourage them to abandon those ways and cultivate the Vinaya.

When one has fully perfected the cultivation of such ethical conduct, the mind becomes free from artifice and deceit, and envy is extinguished. One practices giving oneself and encourages others to do so; one praises giving so that others may practice and learn it; and upon seeing others give, one gives rise to sympathetic joy, without thinking:
"The gift should go to me and not to others."
One should simply reflect:

"Many classes of sentient beings suffer from poverty, hunger, cold, and hardship; may they obtain wealth for happiness in the present life, and through hearing the true Dharma, may they attain happiness in future lives."
"I should now diligently cultivate the path in this life, vowing that all sentient beings may likewise attain liberation.
This is called the bodhisattva’s mind free from envy, which attains equanimity toward all sentient beings.

Whether practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects, they do so for the sake of all sentient beings with a mind free from duality.

Why is this? Because the Dharma one cultivates takes as its object the shared mindfulness of sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly attain the Way; having oneself emerged from the fires of birth and death, one also vows that sentient beings may likewise achieve liberation.
“O Heavenly King!
Suppose a householder has six young sons whom he loves equally, without any partiality.
While the householder is away, a fire breaks out in his home. What do you think?”
At that time, the elder had this thought:
"Should I save my six children one after another?
"No! [the Buddha replied].
World-Honored One!
Why is this? It is because the father’s mind is impartial toward his son.
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
It is the same with the Bodhisattva.
Fools are greedily attached to their abodes within the six realms of existence; they do not know how to escape from this fire-housed of birth and death."
These bodhisattvas, with a mind of equanimity, employ various skillful means to guide and transform them so that they emerge [from suffering], establishing them all within the realm of parinirvāṇa.
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are equal toward all phenomena; they protect the True Dharma and make offerings to the Tathāgata with various kinds of requisites; they make offerings to the Tathāgata through practice according to reality; they benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; they guard the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings; they skillfully guide sentient beings in accordance with their needs; they practice the Bodhisattva path without contradicting their words; and with minds free from weariness, they seek unexcelled enlightenment.
If one can act in this way, it is called making offerings to all Buddhas not with material wealth. Why is this?
Because the Dharma is the body of the Buddha; if one makes offerings to the Dharma, one is making offerings to the Buddha.

All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have come from the practice of suchness; they act solely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, protecting their wholesome dharmas and acting in accordance with them. Were it otherwise, they would violate their original vows; through indolence and laziness, they would be unable to fulfill the mind of bodhi.

Why is this? Because the unsurpassed enlightenment toward which a bodhisattva aspires is shared with sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, how could one possibly attain unsurpassed enlightenment?

“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā and cultivate the offering of the True Dharma to the Tathāgata, this is called the true offering.”

Thus making offerings, he uproots pride (*māna*), distances himself from worldly affairs, and shaves off his beard and hair. Regarding his parents, brothers, and kinsmen, he has no concern for them, as if they were already dead; his appearance and clothing are entirely different from the ordinary, and he wanders into cities and towns carrying his alms-bowl (*pātra*).
Even when he arrives at the home of a *caṇḍāla* relative, he likewise subdues his pride and humbles his mind to beg for food, thinking:
"My life belongs to others; my life is sustained by their gift of food. By this cause and condition, I am able to eliminate my pride."
He further thought:
"I should now act in accordance with the wishes of my teachers and friends to bring them joy;

for the sake of hearing the Dharma that I have not heard before, and if I see others in a state of anger, resentment, or strife, I should immediately practice patience, humble myself, and avoid them."
"In this way, the Bodhisattva eradicates the conceit of 'I' and 'mine.
O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they give rise to firm and correct faith."
Why is this? Because they possess manifold merits;
the power of the roots of goodness planted in past lives is strong;
they are fully endowed with virtuous causes and have accomplished right view.
Not relying on external conditions, the inner mind is pure;
not depending on other teachers, the mental conduct is harmonious and upright;
far removed from flattery and deceit, the faculties are keen and sharp.
Fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are free from all hindrances and obstructions, their minds being pure;
they distance themselves from evil friends and draw near to virtuous friends;
seeking out wholesome speech, they do not give rise to indolence, and upon hearing the Dharma taught, they recognize the merits of the Buddha.
At that time, Varaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that, out of great compassion and pity,
you will explain for us the marks of the Tathāgata’s great majestic power and merit!"
The Buddha told Jiusheng:
"O Devaputra! Listen attentively now!"
"Excellent thought!
I shall explain to you a small portion of the Buddha’s meritorious virtues and majestic spiritual power.
Most Victorious addressed him, saying:
“Indeed! We pray that you will speak;
we long to hear it.”
The Buddha said, “O Heavenly King!

The Tathāgata is endowed with boundless great compassion that universally illumines sentient beings. Encompassing the realm of sentient beings, it even pervades throughout the ten directions to the very limits of space, such that it cannot be measured.”
The Great Compassion of the Tathāgata is something that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas do not possess.

Why is this? Because it is an unshared quality (*āveṇika-dharma*); there is not a single sentient being in the worlds of the ten directions who is not illuminated by the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is ultimately inexhaustible; for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, even after expounding the essentials of all dharmas through various causes and conditions over immeasurable eons, it remains impossible to exhaust them.

Should there be any inquiries regarding the various words and all the meanings of phrases within the realm of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, in the mere twinkling of an eye, provides a distinct analysis for each and every sentient being, such that none can refute him.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s attainment of the unimpeded sphere of meditative concentration, which is profoundly deep and immeasurable: even if all sentient beings in every world-system were to attain the ten stages of a bodhisattva and enter superior samādhi for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they would still be unable to fathom the Tathāgata’s state of meditative absorption.
The body of the Tathāgata is of infinite measure. Why is this?
Because, according to what beings wish to see, he is able to manifest an infinite variety of distinct bodies within a single moment of thought.

The Tathāgata’s divine eye is most supreme and pure; he perceives all the various distinctions of form among all sentient beings in all worlds, as well as the diverse differences among other categories of things, seeing them all as clearly as one would an *āmala* fruit held in the palm of one's hand—something that cannot be attained by the eyes of ordinary people or even by the divine eyes of others.

The Tathāgata’s divine ear is most supreme and pure; all the various sounds of sentient beings, as well as the sounds of all other categories of things, he hears entirely in a single thought-moment and understands their meanings.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses the pure knowledge of others' minds; regarding all sentient beings in all worlds, their individual thoughts, karmic actions, and the infinite distinctions in how they receive the fruits thereof, the Buddha fully understands them all within a single moment of his four modes of conduct.
Why is this? Because the Buddha is always in meditative concentration and free from distraction.
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!
The Buddha has no loss of mindfulness, his mind is not distracted, and his faculties have no other objects.
Why is this? Because he is free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions, being most pure, tranquil, and stainless.
Those who possess afflictions lose mindfulness and become distracted, as their faculties have diverse objects;

the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is untainted and free from defilement, having attained sovereign equality over all dharmas, because he always abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

The Tathāgata abides in but a single mode of deportment, from his wandering in a single samādhi up until his parinirvāṇa; yet even humans and devas cannot know this, let alone any human or deva being able to fully comprehend the Tathāgata’s cultivation of immeasurable and boundless samādhis throughout countless kalpas!
"Why is this? Because the merits of the Tathāgata are immeasurable, inconceivable, and unobservable.
At that time, Varaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have heard that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood after practicing for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). Why do you now say he practiced for immeasurable eons?
The Buddha said, “O Heavenly King!
That meaning is not so. Why is this?

The unsurpassed bodhi toward which a bodhisattva aspires is accomplished only through immeasurable effort; it is not possible to realize and enter the principle of the equality of phenomena without passing through such a number of kalpas. Only when cultivation reaches its ultimate consummation is one called a Buddha.
Thereupon, Most Excellent addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent!”
Excellent!

You have skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma, effectively exhorting and inspiring all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness, distance themselves from karmic obstructions, rejoice in the fruit of Buddhahood, and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s meritorious virtues and majestic spiritual power, give rise to joy in their hearts, accept them with faith, and praise them, you should know that they will before long become vessels for the meritorious virtues and majestic spiritual power of a Buddha; how much more so for those who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, make offerings to, and explain them to others—the merit they obtain is inconceivable!
The Buddha said,
“O Devaputra! It is so!”

It is so! Those classes of sentient beings are protected by the Tathāgata; having planted roots of goodness over many kalpas, and having made offerings to many Buddhas in the past, they are now able to hear of the Buddha’s merits and majestic spiritual power.

"O Heavenly King, you should know that if good men and good women, free from doubt and hesitation, bathe and purify themselves for seven days, put on new and clean garments, and make offerings of flowers and incense while maintaining single-minded right mindfulness of the Tathāgata’s merits and great majestic power as previously described, then at that time the Tathāgata will protect them with compassion, manifest his body so they may see him, and cause their aspirations to be fulfilled."

"If one lacks flowers, incense, or other such offerings, by simply recollecting the merit and majestic spiritual power with a single-minded focus, one will certainly behold the Buddha at the time of death.
At that time, Sujaya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any sentient being who, upon hearing such an account of the Tathāgata’s merits and great majestic spiritual power, would fail to give rise to faith and instead slander it?"
The Buddha said, “There are indeed such cases!

That is to say, there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s meritorious virtues and majestic spiritual power, give rise to unwholesome thoughts of anger and resentment, slandering it; they conceive of the Dharma-preacher as an evil friend. When their lives end, they will inevitably fall into hell and suffer for many eons.”

If sentient beings, upon hearing such accounts of the Tathāgata’s merits and great majestic power, receive them with joy and faith, praise and keep them in mind, and conceive the thought of the Dharma-preacher as a virtuous friend;
they will, after their lives end, certainly ascend to the realms of humans or devas, progressing ever upward until they attain Buddhahood.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, first covering his own face, then his head, then his entire body, then the lion throne, then the assembly of bodhisattvas, then the assembly of śrāvakas, and finally covering the entire great assembly—including Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, non-humans, and others—before withdrawing his tongue and addressing the great assembly:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses such a tongue-mark; how could he ever speak falsely?"
"You, the great assembly, should all believe and accept what I have spoken; thus you shall obtain peace for a long night.

When this Dharma was spoken, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas among the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); immeasurable sentient beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye; and countless sentient beings all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 568. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Six: Chapter on the Nature of Phenomena (Dharmatā-parivarta). At that time, the Most Victorious One rose again from his seat, draped his upper robe over his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare! How marvelous!"
World-Honored One!

You have well expounded the subtle and wondrous merits as well as the great majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas. By what causes and conditions do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain these subtle and wondrous merits and great majestic spiritual power?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this!
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
“O Heavenly King, you should know!”
"The conduct of the Tathāgata and the fruit he has attained are profoundly deep, subtle, and inconceivable.
Most Victorious addressed him, saying:
"By what dharma does the Buddha's conduct become profound, subtle, and inconceivable?"
The Buddha said:

“The causal nature of the Tathāgata’s dharma is profoundly deep, subtle, and inconceivable; likewise, his meritorious spiritual power and the benefit and joy he brings to others through the teachings he proclaims are also thus.”
The Most Victorious One spoke again:
"In what way is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) profound, subtle, and inconceivable?
The Buddha said:

“O Deva! The *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata exists within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*) of sentient beings. From beginningless time, it has been transmitted in succession; it is unstained by afflictions and its intrinsic nature is pure. It cannot be conditioned by mind, intellect, or consciousness; it cannot be discriminated by other discursive thoughts or investigations; it cannot be the object of false mindfulness or conceptualization. Being far removed from false mindfulness, ignorance does not arise. Therefore, it is called ‘signless’ (*animitta*) because it does not proceed from the twelve links of dependent origination. It is a non-conditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), unborn, unceasing, boundless, inexhaustible, and eternally abiding in its own characteristic.”
"O Heavenly King,

you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus pure— unstained, unattached, and far removed from defilement— and is completely liberated, transcending all afflictions."
This nature is precisely what is called the root of all Buddha-dharmas; from it arise the causes of merit and wisdom. Its original nature is luminous, pure, and inconceivable.
O Heavenly King!
"I shall now speak a parable; you should listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
The king said:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed! We pray that you will speak!”
The Buddha told Jiusheng:
"Great King, you should know!

It is like a priceless wish-fulfilling jewel, polished and refined until it is bright, pure, and lovely; its substance is perfectly round and clean, free from any stain or turbidity. Suppose it fell into the mud long ago, and someone found it, took it with joy, and guarded it with diligent effort so that it would not fall again."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise: though it exists amidst afflictions, it is not defiled by them, and subsequently manifests again.
O Heavenly King!
All Buddhas know that the fundamental nature of sentient beings is pure, yet they are unable to realize this because it is obscured by adventitious afflictions.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should form this thought:
"I shall diligently expound the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of sentient beings, removing their afflictions and enabling them to attain realization and entry."
"All sentient beings are pure by nature; one should give rise to reverence for them and not treat them with contempt, but should honor them according to the Dharma as if they were the Great Teacher.
By forming such thoughts, these bodhisattvas are able to give rise to prajñā and great compassion;
practicing the profound perfection of wisdom in this way, the bodhisattva is then able to realize and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, further reflect:
"These afflictions are powerless, incapable, inherently false, and contrary to the pure dharmas."
Why is this? Because they turn their backs on all-knowledge and follow along with birth and death.
The pure *dharmatā* is the foundation of all phenomena; its own nature has no foundation. False and delusive afflictions all arise from erroneous thoughts and inversions.
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!
For example, just as the four great elements are established in dependence upon space, yet space has no support;
so too it is with afflictions, which depend upon the dharma-nature, yet the dharma-nature has no support."

When these bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they observe and know reality as it is, giving rise to no opposition; because they act in accordance with reality, afflictions do not arise.
These bodhisattvas observe afflictions without giving rise to attachment, thinking:
"If I myself were attached, how could I teach the Dharma to enable others to attain liberation?"
Therefore, the bodhisattva eliminates the mind of attachment and teaches the Dharma according to reality to liberate sentient beings from their bonds.
These bodhisattvas further reflect:
"If there were even a single affliction within the cycle of birth and death that could benefit sentient beings, I would embrace it; however, since no such thing exists, it must be eliminated."
These bodhisattvas further thought:
"Just as the Buddhas of the past practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and severed all afflictions, so too should I."
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, when they were formerly on the causal ground, also studied in this way and thereby accomplished Bodhi.
By means of these two conditions, these bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, observe and know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Thus, this dharmatā is immeasurable and boundless, yet it is obscured and covered by various afflictions; following the stream of birth and death, it sinks into the six destinies and revolves through the long night. Because it follows sentient beings, it is called the "nature of sentient beings."
"O Heavenly King, you should know!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they give rise to a mind of weary detachment, eliminate desire for the five sensory objects, extinguish all conceptual discriminations, and cultivate the unsurpassed path. At that time, this nature is called 'renunciation' (*niḥsaraṇa*); because it transcends all suffering, it is called 'quiescence' (*śānti*). This is the ultimate dharma sought after by the world; the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is eternally abiding and subtle. By means of this dharma-nature, one can attain mastery and receive the rank of Dharma King."

“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they observe the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) throughout the initial, middle, and final stages as entirely equal and originally quiescent. They are not obstructed by any phenomena, just as space is not obstructed by form.”

These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, perceive and know as they truly are all the sublime practices taught by the Buddhas, cultivating them according to their measure. The qualities of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be fully described; they are without the two marks of duality, transcending the spheres of identity and difference. They are of a single, equal mark, wherein discursive thought and investigation do not operate.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they are able to eliminate two marks:
the mark of a self (*ātman*) and the mark of phenomena (*dharma*).
All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), bound by grasping, do not recognize, do not see, and do not attain the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
When these bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to penetrate this nature of phenomena as being non-dual and undifferentiated among all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena has no differentiated characteristics.
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate all roots of goodness based on this dharma-nature; they enter the three realms of existence to benefit sentient beings, and although they manifest impermanence, it is not ultimately real.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and, by observing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as it truly is, they are fully endowed with the power of skillful means, great compassion, and their vows, and thus do not abandon sentient beings;

whereas those of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings lack such power of great compassion and vows, and therefore do not perceive the perfectly pure nature of phenomena and are unable to benefit sentient beings in accordance with reality.

“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to contemplate the truly pure nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in this manner.”

All noble ones enter into this reality as it truly is: there is no one who can practice, nor any dharma to be practiced; there is no one who can act, nor any dharma to be acted upon; there is no mind and no mental factors; there is no karma and no maturation; there is no suffering and no pleasure.

One who contemplates in this manner is said to have attained equanimity; it is non-dual, free from attachment, and conforms to the vast. It is without self or what belongs to self, without high or low, truly inexhaustible, eternally abiding, luminous, and pure.
Why is this so? Because all the noble dharmas are accomplished by means of this;

it is because of this nature that the noble ones manifest. The boundless qualities and unshared dharmas of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, arise from this nature and emerge from this nature. All the categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom of the noble ones arise from this nature, and the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerges from this nature.

This nature is quiescent, transcending all names and signs; its nature is reality, far removed from inversion; because its nature is immutable, it is called *tathatā* (suchness); because it is the domain of noble wisdom, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, neither defiled nor pure; it is free from unity and free from difference, signless and nameless.
“O Heavenly King, you should know!
These bodhisattvas further reflect thus:
‘The nature of phenomena is free from characteristics; all phenomena are free from characteristics, non-dual and without distinction.’”

Why is this? Because the signlessness of all phenomena is the signlessness of the dharma-nature; the signlessness of the dharma-nature is the signlessness of sentient beings; the signlessness of sentient beings is the signlessness of the dharma-realm; and the signlessness of the dharma-realm is the signlessness of all phenomena. Thus, these signs of departure cannot be apprehended through seeking.
The suchness of the nature of phenomena and the suchness of sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction;

the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the nature of phenomena are non-dual and without distinction; the suchness of the nature of phenomena and the suchness of all dharmas are non-dual and without distinction;
the suchness of all dharmas and the suchness of all Buddhas are non-dual and without distinction—the suchness of the nature of phenomena.
The suchness of the three periods of time is not in conflict; the suchness of the past is not in conflict with the suchness of the future,
the suchness of the future is not in conflict with the suchness of the present,
the suchness of the present is not in conflict with the suchness of the past, and the suchness of the three periods of time is identical to the aggregates and the elements.
Abiding in suchness: the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases is the suchness of defilement and purity;
the suchness of defilement and purity is the suchness of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; and the suchness of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is the suchness of all phenomena.
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
Suchness (*tathatā*) is called non-differentiation, non-alteration, non-arising, and non-contention; its self-nature is reality. Because it is free from contention, it is termed 'Suchness.

To know and see all phenomena as they truly are—namely, that they do not arise—and though phenomena arise, Suchness remains unmoved; and though Suchness gives rise to all phenomena, Suchness itself does not arise—this is called the Dharma-body."

Pure and unchanging like space, it is peerless; among all things within the three realms, there is not a single dharma that can equal it, nor is there anything that can compare to it throughout the bodies of all sentient beings.

Pure and free from defilement, it is primordially unstained; its self-nature is luminous and pure, its self-nature is unborn, and its self-nature is unarisen. It is neither within mind, intellect, or consciousness, nor is it mind, intellect, or consciousness; its nature is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Pervading the entire realm of space and the abodes of all sentient beings, it is entirely equal—immeasurable, boundless, non-different, and non-distinct.

It is not form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is not the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind, yet it is not separate from the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind;
it is without birth, yet it is not separate from birth;
though it goes against the flow of birth and death, it does not conform to nirvana.
The eye cannot see, the ear cannot hear, the nose cannot smell, the tongue cannot taste, the body cannot feel, and the mind cannot cognize;
it is not within the mind, intellect, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from the mind, intellect, or consciousness.
"O Heavenly King, you should know that this is called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Because the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and are able to penetrate this nature of phenomena, their cultivation is pure; they are thus able to manifest physical bodies within all the Jambudvīpa cities, towns, and villages throughout the trichiliocosm."

The body manifested is neither form nor characteristic, yet it manifests forms and characteristics; although it is not an object within the range of the six sense faculties, it constantly transforms sentient beings without rest. It teaches that this body is impermanent, non-self, suffering, and impure. Because it knows that all sentient beings possess the nature of quiescence, it manifests immeasurable kinds of bodies, employing skillful means to bring them to transformation. Knowing that all bodies have no agent and no experiencer, being like wood or stone, it nevertheless teaches pure conduct for the sake of sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and thereby attain mastery. Without shifting from that state, they initiate the activities of wisdom, sporting with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and manifesting various displays. Abiding in such mastery, they can manifest various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), and through their sovereignty, they proceed toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), fully penetrating the nature of all phenomena.
"O Heavenly King, you should know!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses such sovereignty as this: it is the mark of inexhaustibility; it pervades all places, manifesting form where there is no form; it sovereignly and universally contemplates the minds of all sentient beings, seeing the true nature of the mind as it is; it sovereignly recollects boundless and countless eons in an uninterrupted continuity; it sovereignly manifests transformations; it dwells in the mark of liberation and sovereignly attains the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), yet for the sake of sentient beings, it does not realize that exhaustion of outflows but sovereignly transcends the world; it is the realm of noble wisdom, sovereignly profound, such that *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* cannot fathom it; it is sovereignly firm and indestructible by Māra; seated upon the *bodhimaṇḍa*, it is the foremost in accomplishing the Buddha-dharma; it sovereignly accords with conditions to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; it sovereignly tames and transforms all sentient beings; and it sovereignly receives the consecration, attaining mastery over all dharmas.

"O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as it truly is; having attained this mastery and cultivated this mastery, they immediately acquire all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*), remaining unbound by the three realms."
Why is this? Because they have distanced themselves from all false conceptualization, the fetters of affliction, and inverted attachments to signs.
If they wish to take birth, they possess mastery over birth and remain free from bondage.
If they wish to manifest cessation, they possess mastery over cessation; wherever they are born, they constantly embrace the Mahāyāna to mature the Buddha-dharma.

They are able to search for the Buddha-dharma throughout the ten directions and find it ultimately unobtainable, knowing that all phenomena are one with the Buddha-dharma—neither eternal nor annihilated.
Why is this? Because when one investigates this dharma, it cannot be apprehended; it cannot be apprehended when sought through the principle of suchness (*yathābhūta*).

This dharma cannot be said to exist or not to exist, nor does it possess names or signs beyond this sphere of experience. If one is free from names and signs, that is equality; if dharmas are equal, there is no attachment. That which is without anything to be attached to is the reality of dharmas. If one clings to reality, that is falsehood; because there is no clinging, it is not false. When there is no stagnation or attachment, the mind is unimpeded; being unimpeded, there is no obstruction; being without obstruction, there is no contention. If dharmas are without contention, they are identical to space and are not bound to the three realms.

If all things are without attachment or connection, these phenomena are formless, signless, and shapeless; if phenomena are formless, signless, and shapeless, one should know that such phenomena, in accordance with their respective objects, are free from both the knower and the known.

Why is this? Because within this there is not the slightest dharma that can be awakened to, nor the slightest dharma that can awaken; this is called the bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and penetrating equality.
“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate and give rise to great loving-kindness,
great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, yet they do not perceive a self, nor do they perceive sentient beings.”
...up to not perceiving a knower or a seer; though practicing generosity, there is nothing relinquished;
though upholding pure ethical discipline, one is free from the marks of discipline; though cultivating patience, the mind is inexhaustible;
though cultivating diligence, one is free from its marks; though cultivating meditative concentration, there is no object of stilling; and though cultivating wisdom—
Yet there is no object of focus; though one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, there is nothing grasped; though one cultivates the right efforts, the mind is equanimous;
though one cultivates the bases of psychic power, one is free from conceptual proliferation;

though one cultivates the faculties and powers, one does not discriminate among the faculties of sentient beings and remains free from faults; though one cultivates the factors of enlightenment, there is no discrimination. Though...
One cultivates the factors of the path without effort; though one cultivates pure faith, one remains without attachment.
One naturally possesses the wisdom that recollects the mind of equality regarding all phenomena; one cultivates sublime concentrations with a non-conceptual mind;
one observes sublime wisdom with an unceasing mind; one cultivates śamatha with a mind free from seeing; and one cultivates vipaśyanā...
With a mind free from conceptualization, one cultivates the recollection of the Buddha, attaining a mind that penetrates the equality of the dharma-realm;

one cultivates the recollection of the Dharma with a mind that dwells nowhere; one cultivates the recollection of the Sangha with a fundamentally pure mind, teaching and transforming sentient beings without giving rise to discrimination.

The mind of the Dharma-realm encompasses all phenomena; with a mind like space, one adorns and purifies Buddha-lands; with a mind that has nothing to attain, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); with a mind free from advancing or retreating, one attains non-retrogression; with a mind far removed from signs, one does not perceive the existence of signs; with a mind of equality toward the three realms, one adorns the Bodhi seat; with a mind of no awakening, one knows all phenomena; though one turns the wheel of Dharma, one perceives neither speaker nor listener; and though one manifests nirvana, one knows that the fundamental nature of birth and death is equal.

“O Heavenly King, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they contemplate phenomena in this way: they do not perceive a subject that contemplates, nor do they perceive an object that is contemplated; at that very moment, they are able to attain mastery in playful sport.”
Why is this? Because when one's own mind is pure, one is able to see all sentient beings as pure.
O Heavenly King, you should know this!
"Just as space pervades all things, so too is the mind of these bodhisattvas practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

While this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand devas and humans among the assembly simultaneously resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand sentient beings became free from dust and removed from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye; and for twelve thousand bhikṣus, all outflows were forever exhausted."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Deva Varapravara, saying:
"O Heavenly King, you should know!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds attain purity as deep as the great ocean; their merit and wisdom are immeasurable, and they are able to manifest the jewels of supramundane virtues. Sentient beings may utilize them until they reach *bodhi* without them ever being exhausted, yet the merit of the Bodhisattva likewise does not diminish."

Just as the great ocean produces many kinds of precious jewels, the wisdom of a bodhisattva is profoundly deep and difficult to enter; neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas are able to traverse it. Furthermore, just as small animals do not enter the great ocean, the wisdom of a bodhisattva is vast and boundless.
Why is this? Because it is without attachment, without dwelling, without form, and without marks.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva becomes progressively deeper from beginning to end: first is the bodhicitta, and finally is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

It is the natural law for Bodhisattvas not to dwell with afflictions or evil associates. If worldly wisdom enters the ocean of Bodhisattva wisdom, it becomes of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, signlessness—and flows toward the non-conceptual flavor of omniscience.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena and perceives neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly realized the profound nature of the equality of all dharmas.

The power of the great compassion possessed by Bodhisattvas does not contradict their original vows; it is the locus upon which all noble ones rely, and for the sake of all sentient beings, they preach the Dharma through eternal kalpas without end.
"O Devaputra!
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they penetrate such a deeply profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
O Devaputra!"

The Bodhisattva is skillfully able to penetrate the dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Although they speak of various forms (*rūpa*), these do not truly exist; when investigating these forms, they ultimately do not grasp or cling to them. It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although they speak of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), it does not truly exist; when investigating the earth element, they ultimately do not grasp or cling to it. It is the same for the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. Although they speak of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), it does not truly exist;
when investigating the eye-base, they ultimately do not grasp or cling to it. It is the same for the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Although the sense-base of form is taught, it does not exist in reality; when one investigates the sense-base of form, one ultimately does not grasp at it, and the same applies to the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
Although the self is taught, it does not exist in reality; when one investigates this self, one ultimately does not grasp at it, and the same applies to sentient beings up to the knower and the seer.
Although the world is taught, it does not exist in reality; when one investigates the world, one ultimately does not grasp at it.
Although worldly phenomena are spoken of, they do not truly exist; yet when one investigates worldly phenomena, one ultimately does not grasp them.
Although the Buddha-dharma is spoken of, it does not truly exist; yet when one investigates the Buddha-dharma, one ultimately does not grasp it.
Although bodhi is spoken of, it does not truly exist; yet when one investigates bodhi, one ultimately does not grasp it.

“O Heavenly King, you should know that whatever is expressed through speech is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this is not ultimate reality. If there were no conventional truth, it would be impossible to speak of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).”

These bodhisattvas penetrate conventional truth without contradicting ultimate truth; by virtue of this penetration, they know that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, without formation or disintegration, and without "this" or "that," remaining far removed from the conceptual proliferation of language and letters.

"O Deva, you should know that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is beyond words and quiescent; it is the domain of noble wisdom (āryajñāna), a dharma that is unchanging and indestructible. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, its essential nature and characteristics remain eternally constant. This is called the Bodhisattva’s thorough penetration of the ultimate truth."
At that time, Ajita addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, and are empty and detached by their very nature, how can there be the appearance of a Buddha in the world and the turning of the wheel of Dharma?"
"How is it that a bodhisattva perceives arising within dharmas that are unarisen?
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
"O Heavenly King, you should know this!"
All phenomena are without cessation; therefore, they are without arising.
Why is this? Because their nature is unchanging. It is only through conventional perception that arising and cessation are seen; these are all false and not truly existent.

If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they employ skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to perceive the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). They know that conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is empty and non-existent, lacking any solid reality; it appears to exist though it does not truly exist, being like a phantom, a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, a magical creation, or a city of the gandharvas—unstable and flickering, arising from causes and conditions. These bodhisattvas, through sublime *prajñā*, contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena, explaining at length that they arise from causes and conditions, and reflect as follows:
"These various phenomena are now seen to have arising, abiding, and ceasing; by what causes and conditions do they arise?"

"By what causes and conditions does cessation occur? Having reflected thus, he understood as it truly is: "With ignorance as a cause and condition, volitional formations arise; depending on volitional formations, consciousness arises; and so on, in detail, until: because of existence, birth arises; from birth come old age, and because of old age come death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."

Therefore, one practices cultivation in order to sever ignorance; once ignorance is severed, the remaining eleven links perish in succession, just as when the body is severed, life and the other faculties perish accordingly.

"Great King, you should know that those heterodox practitioners with wrong views, seeking liberation, merely wish to sever death without knowing how to sever birth; yet if a phenomenon does not arise, it cannot cease."

For example, if someone throws a clod of earth at a lion, the lion pursues the person and the clod naturally comes to rest; so it is with the Bodhisattva, who merely cuts off rebirth and thus death ceases of its own accord.

A dog, however, only chases the clod and does not know to chase the person; thus the clod never comes to rest. The non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*) are likewise: not knowing how to cut off rebirth, they will never escape death.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they skillfully understand the arising and ceasing of all phenomena through causes and conditions.

"O Heavenly King, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they realize that dependently arisen phenomena are empty and non-existent, and thus they do not give rise to the conceit of 'I'."
If born into a wealthy and noble family, one does not give rise to the two types of pride—arrogance regarding wealth and arrogance regarding status.

If born into a poor and lowly family, one recognizes that because one’s past karma was not particularly pure, the resulting fruit is inferior; thus, a mind of weary detachment arises and one seeks to leave the household life, forming this thought:
"Since this body of mine was obtained through mixed karma, I shall further cultivate pure karma to make myself pure, and cause others to do likewise."
"Having sought deliverance for myself, I shall likewise deliver others; having sought my own liberation, I shall also untie the bonds of others.

For these reasons, one should arouse diligence and distance oneself from indolence; all unwholesome dharmas that obstruct the Path should be abandoned, and all wholesome dharmas that assist the Path should be increased. Diligently cultivating vigor, one should reflect thus: "I bear a heavy burden;
I must personally extinguish all afflictions and deliver sentient beings, and I must not be indolent."

"These bodhisattvas draw near to their teachers—whether those with extensive learning or little learning, those with wisdom or without wisdom, those who uphold the precepts or have broken them—and regard them all as Buddhas, honoring them as fellow students. They reflect:

'Now, relying upon my teacher to study and learn, I must bring to fulfillment whatever wholesome qualities I have not yet fulfilled; I must sever and exhaust whatever afflictions I have not yet exhausted; I shall guard the wholesome dharmas and abandon the unwholesome; I shall possess all-knowledge, have compassion for the world, become a field of merit through great compassion, and bring my afflictions to stillness.'"
"The Teacher of Gods and Humans is my Great Master; he has excellently attained supreme victory, and all gods and humans serve the Lord of Dharma as their Great Master.
These bodhisattvas reflect in this way:
"The Buddha has taught the pure precepts; even for the sake of body or life, we shall not violate them."
As the World-Honored One has said:
"To comply with the Buddha's teaching is itself to make offerings to the Buddha, the brahmins, and others.

To provide various foods and drinks with a faithful mind, and for them to be used according to the Dharma, ensures that the person does not receive fruitless results; both the eater and the donor alike obtain benefit."
“Brahmins and others, by using the name ‘śramaṇa,’ conceive of the Bodhisattva as a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
The Bodhisattva should practice the True Dharma according to principle and measure, thereby manifesting the virtues of a śramaṇa and the virtues of a field of merit.”

In this way, the bodhisattvas practice for themselves and transform others without ever ceasing or abandoning their efforts. When these bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, such cultivation enables them to accord with all the world:

seeing those who are angry and resentful, they give rise to a mind of humility; seeing those who are arrogant, they give rise to the perception of non-self; seeing those who are crooked and deviant, they give rise to the perception of uprightness; seeing those who speak deceptively, they give rise to truthful speech; toward those who speak harshly, they always utter words of loving-kindness; seeing those who are stubborn and rigid, they manifest gentleness; seeing those who are cruel and poisonous, they give rise to compassionate patience; seeing those who follow false teachings, they give rise to great kindness (*maitrī*); seeing those who suffer and are distressed, they give rise to great compassion (*karuṇā*); and seeing those who are stingy and envious, they practice generosity (*dāna*).
These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, give birth in pure buddha-fields because they thus accord with worldly knowledge. Why is this?

Maintaining the precepts without deficiency and remaining free from all impurities, they cultivate a mind of equanimity; toward sentient beings, they possess great roots of goodness and do not cling to fame or profit. Having pure faith, they harbor no expectations; they practice diligence with vigor, never giving rise to indolence. They cultivate various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) to remain free from the states of distraction, and through subtle wisdom, they practice extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). With unimpaired faculties and endowed with sharp intelligence, they constantly cultivate great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and remain far removed from anger and affliction. By these causes and conditions, they are born in a pure Buddha-land.
At that time, Ajita addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Regarding what the Buddha has taught—that by practicing the dharmas such as the precepts one is born in a pure buddha-field—is it necessary to practice them all together, or will one be born in a pure buddha-field by practicing even a single one?"
The Buddha told Jiusheng:
“Great King, you should know!

If there is a bodhisattva who, among the various teachings previously mentioned, purely cultivates even one single practice, they will thereby fulfill all dharmas; through such a single practice, they shall likewise be born in a pure land.”
Why is this? Because within each and every practice, all practices are fully contained.
These bodhisattvas are born in pure buddha-fields and are not defiled by the womb.

Why is this? These bodhisattvas fashion images of the Buddha and cultivate monastic gardens; before the stūpas of the Buddha, they smear the ground with fragrant clay and offer incense, or scatter exquisite flowers, or bathe the Buddha images with fragrant water. Within the monastic gardens, they sweep, sprinkle, and plaster the floors. With a heart of compassion, they serve and attend upon their parents, teachers, and the Saṃgha; toward their fellow students, virtuous friends, and all śramaṇas, they offer respectful service with a mind of equanimity. Taking these roots of goodness, they share them with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so that all sentient beings may attain purity. In this way, the bodhisattva attains freedom from desire.

Why is this? Because their minds are free from grasping and attachment, untainted by partisanship, and they turn their backs on all sensory objects while remaining far removed from the conditions of craving. Their hearts are not stained by attachment to the realm of exquisite desires; they practice the precepts taught by the Buddha according to reality; they have few desires and are content with the four requisites of life; they always feel dread regarding the acquisition of the physical body and mind; and they constantly delight in the dharma of tranquility and seclusion.

"In this way, the bodhisattva does not cling to worldly affairs and thereby attains a pure livelihood, free from hypocrisy in demeanor and deceitful speech or thought. That is to say, in the presence of a donor, he never feigns virtue; he walks slowly and steadily, looking ahead a distance of six cubits, without glancing left or right at the deportment of one who seeks gain through wrong livelihood.

When no donor is present, he immediately becomes dissolute. Furthermore, in the presence of a donor, he does not use subtle or pleasant words to flatter them for the sake of profit; when no donor is present, his speech becomes coarse and vulgar.
Seeing others practicing giving, he conceals his actual greed by saying it is unnecessary, and he becomes resentful if he does not receive anything."
They speak of having few desires while their hearts are full of greed for profit.
These bodhisattvas do not possess such signs of seeking gain; even if they see a donor, they never say:
"My three robes are worn out, my utensils are lacking, or I need medicine."
Furthermore, in the presence of a donor, one should never say:

"This donor gave me this object; that person says I uphold the precepts, am learned, and possess a pure heart of great compassion. Even if they thus praise me, I have no such virtues; I shall only diligently cultivate goodness to repay the donor's kindness.

"These bodhisattvas do not seek fame or profit by praising themselves and disparaging others in the presence of laypeople; they do not give rise to anger or resentment when seeing others receive offerings; they never use flattery or crookedness to acquire wealth; they do not feign intimacy to harm others and take their property; nor do they hope for the humiliation of others or use mockery to obtain wealth."

Whether the donor intends to give to those who have been praised, or to the Dharma-preacher, or to the great assembly, or if the recipient has not yet been specifically designated, or if the gift has not yet been finalized, the Bodhisattva will never enter among them to take a share.
If one receives gifts of wealth, one should never be attached to them, thinking, "This is my property; this is mine.
Instead, one should immediately redirect them for the equal enjoyment of other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, teachers, monks, parents, and others who are poor and destitute.
If their wealth is exhausted, they do not regard it as a cause for sorrow; even if they receive nothing for a short time, their minds remain free from distress.
These bodhisattvas—whether receiving offerings from others or redirecting them to others—are pure in both cases; because their conduct is pure, their minds do not grow weary.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, dwell long within saṃsāra without weariness; even when beset by demonic activities or manifold sufferings, their minds do not regress.

If there are those who wish to practice the path of the two vehicles, they preach the Dharma for them without shrinking from toil; and as the bodhisattvas themselves cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), they never grow weary.
"When these bodhisattvas practice with such diligence, they are able to act in accordance with the Buddha’s true teaching.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas remain far removed from negligence; their minds are always cautious, and they skillfully restrain their bodies so as not to commit any evil, and the same applies to their speech and thoughts."

Though dwelling in the present, one should always fear the future; severing all unwholesome dharmas so they never arise again, one’s speech must accord with principle, constantly preaching the Dharma teachings while refraining from speaking what is not the Dharma. Abandoning defiled and impure karma, one cultivates pure conduct, does not disparage the Buddha’s teachings, and remains far removed from the impure dharmas of affliction. This is how one protects and upholds the Tathāgata’s true teaching, severing and abandoning all evils and unwholesomeness.
"These bodhisattvas, thus conforming to the pure teachings of the Buddha, when they see sentient beings, display a serene countenance and a smile, remaining free from frowning. Why is this so?..."

With the mind free from defilement and the sense faculties purified, being devoid of the stain of ill-will and having no internal knots of resentment, the Bodhisattva thus attains great learning and observes birth and death.

He is able to know, as it truly is, how the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion burn and cause confusion; he likewise truly awakens to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), the suffering inherent in all formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), and the selflessness of all dharmas (*dharma-nairātmya*). He further perceives that sentient beings in the world are addicted to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and he truly awakens to the fact that among all dharmas, only nirvāṇa is supremely tranquil. Upon hearing others preach the Dharma, he is immediately able to contemplate its meaning and transmit it to others; he gives rise to great compassion and firm mindfulness, for were he not to hear the Dharma, there would be no contemplation or cultivation.
Therefore, the wisdom derived from hearing is like the foundation of all letters; all other forms of wisdom arise because of it.
Having acquired much learning, one then protects the True Dharma.

If, in future ages when the True Dharma is on the verge of extinction, there are sentient beings who delight in diligent practice but do not encounter the torch of the Dharma, and no one is there to expound for them the essential points of the profound teaching;

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately proclaimed the profound Prajñāpāramitā for them, causing all sentient beings to cultivate ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he then praised them, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

At a time when such a true Dharma is perishing, you are able to resolve upon bodhicitta and seek unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; through this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, the sphere of practice of all Buddhas of the three times, if you cultivate it diligently, great awakening will not be far off.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is not separate from great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Just as when a person sows grain and its sprouts have already emerged, one should know that this person will obtain the fruit before long; so it is with the bodhisattva: having sought great enlightenment and now heard the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that they are certainly not far from Buddhahood.
"O sons of good family!
If there are those who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead seek unsurpassed enlightenment by relying on other sūtras, it is absolutely impossible that they could ever realize it."
For example, if a prince were to abandon his father the king and seek to become a crown prince under another person, it would certainly be impossible;
so it is with a bodhisattva: one must rely on the *prajñāpāramitā* to seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), for if one relies on other sūtras, one will certainly not attain it.
For example, just as a calf that desires milk must rely upon its mother—since it cannot obtain it from any other cow—so too it is with a bodhisattva:
one who seeks great enlightenment must rely upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), for if one relies upon other dharmas, one will certainly be unable to realize it.
“O Heavenly King, you should know!

Those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who draw near to the Prajñāpāramitā are the Dharma Princes; their bodies are adorned with the marks and signs, their faculties are unimpaired, they practice the conduct of the Buddhas, and they awaken to that which the Buddhas have awakened to. They rescue and protect all sentient beings afflicted by suffering, skillfully penetrate the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, constantly cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya), remain far removed from defilement and turbidity, and guard the city of omniscience of all Buddhas. These Bodhisattvas, as Dharma Princes, are honored and respected by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World Protectors.”

Why is this? Having practiced the bodhisattva path and attained non-retrogression, they cannot be shaken by any evil māras; they dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma, penetrate the principle of the equality of all emptiness, and do not rely on external conditions.
Abiding thus in the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, which is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they transcend the world and dwell in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

These bodhisattvas are able to know, as it truly is, the distinctions among the superior, middling, and inferior categories of greed, hatred, and delusion in all sentient beings; they likewise know, as it truly is, the distinctions among the categories of wholesome and steadfast minds.
Having known them as they truly are, they teach each being the various gates of remedial methods; in this way, they are skillfully able to transform sentient beings.
Among these bodhisattvas, if there are sentient beings who should be liberated by seeing the body of a Buddha, they immediately manifest the body of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them;
if there are those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a bodhisattva, they manifest the body of a bodhisattva and preach the Dharma for them.
To those who attain liberation upon seeing the body of a Pratyekabuddha, he manifests the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma to them;
to those who attain liberation upon seeing the body of a Śrāvaka, he manifests the body of a Śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma to them;
and if there are those who attain liberation upon seeing the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, elders, or householders, he manifests all such bodies and preaches the Dharma to them.
Bodhisattvas who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) transform all sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation.

These bodhisattvas possess minds that are compassionate, harmonious, upright, gentle, and kind; they are free from the defilements of flattery, crookedness, jealousy, and envy; their minds are always pure and free from coarse or evil speech; and they frequently practice patience while remaining close and familiar with sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they abide in peace and happiness. Why is this?

Because they are fully endowed with right view and pure vision, as well as pure conduct; their sphere of activity accords with their mind, and they do not frequent defiled places where there are spheres of evil and unwholesome dharmas that conflict with the mind.

"These bodhisattvas see their fellow practitioners with deep joy; whether it be material wealth or the Dharma, they enjoy them together, practicing only the Buddha-way and taking only the Buddha as their teacher."

In this way, the bodhisattva dwells in peace and happiness, and possessing the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), he integrates sentient beings: by giving benefit, whether through the gift of peace and happiness or the inexhaustible gift, he integrates sentient beings; by beneficial speech, whether through meaningful speech, speech in accordance with the Dharma, or non-deceptive speech, he integrates sentient beings; and by equality in material benefit, whether through equality in physical benefit, equality in the benefit of life, or equality in the benefit of requisites, he integrates sentient beings.

“O Heavenly King, you should know this: the gift of benefit is the gift of Dharma; the gift of peace and happiness is the gift of material wealth; and the inexhaustible gift is the demonstration of the right path.

Beneficial speech causes the arising of wholesome dharmas; meaningful speech causes one to see the correct principle; speech in accordance with the Dharma follows the Buddha’s teaching; and non-contradictory speech expounds the Dharma as it truly is.”

Equality in material benefit refers to food, drink, clothing, and the like; equality in physical benefit refers to protecting and benefiting one's own body such that others are likewise benefited; equality in life-sustaining benefit refers to various precious gems, which are called "external life"; and equality in the benefit of requisites refers to all pure wealth, such as elephants, horses, and so forth.
These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are equal in their practice both for themselves and for others.

These bodhisattvas are born with handsome features; they are always able to cultivate a tranquil deportment, an unfeigned deportment, and a pure deportment. They are a joy for all to behold, being warm and kind both inwardly and outwardly; those who gaze upon them never grow weary, as they delight the minds of others. All sentient beings love and respect them; those who see them give rise to wholesome thoughts, and even those who were angry and resentful find their hearts reconciled upon seeing them.

These bodhisattvas are thus upright and worthy of being relied upon; they impartially protect sentient beings so that their afflictions are extinguished, and they are able to lead sentient beings out of birth and death. They can ferry sentient beings across the boundless wilderness; for those in the perils of the world who have no kinsmen, they act as friends; for those afflicted by the disease of afflictions, they act as skilled physicians; for those without protection, they act as protectors; for those without refuge, they act as a refuge; and for sentient beings obscured by ignorance, they act as a Dharma-torch.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva serves as a refuge for all sentient beings, skillfully healing their manifold ailments like the king of medicinal trees.
Just as there is a king of trees named Sudarśana, whose roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits can heal diseases through their color, fragrance, taste, and texture;
so too are these Bodhisattvas, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the ultimate goal, constantly healing the sickness of afflictions for sentient beings."

Bodhisattvas possess abundant merit and wisdom; all who see or hear them have their various ailments healed. These bodhisattvas, endowed with such virtues, provide offerings to the Triple Gem according to their capacity.

To those afflicted by illness, they bestow medicine; seeing those hungry or thirsty, they give food and drink; to those suffering from cold, they provide clothing. They serve their preceptors and instructors with all their heart, and show reverent salutation with palms joined to their fellow practitioners of the Dharma. They construct monasteries and donate gardens and fields, giving away whatever wealth and resources they have from time to time. They manage their servants and slaves in accordance with the Dharma, and whenever they hear of those of renowned virtue—brahmins, śramaṇas, or practitioners of the right path—they visit them for consultation at regular intervals.

"These bodhisattvas are able to generate manifold virtues and employ skillful means to transform and deliver sentient beings. While remaining in this buddha-field without their bodies wavering, they travel to the worlds of infinite buddhas to receive the sublime Dharma from those buddhas and bodhisattvas. They may manifest making offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas; or manifest practicing the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); or manifest making offerings to those who have newly attained buddhahood; or manifest themselves attaining equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); or manifest turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma for the masses; or manifest entering parinirvāṇa to provide great benefit; or manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) for those who are ready to be delivered, causing them all to behold these forms and obtain benefit and joy.
Although they perform such various buddha-activities, they do so without mental effort and without conceptual discrimination."
At that time, Ajita addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How is it that these bodhisattvas perform various transformations with a mind free from discrimination?"
The Buddha said,
"O Deva-king!
It is like the sun and moon, which, though they illuminate all things, do not form discriminations."
"I emit radiance that is able to illuminate.
Yet, it is by the power of their own karma that sentient beings experience the sun and moon circling and illuminating day and night;
these Bodhisattvas are likewise: although they manifest transformation bodies, they remain free from conceptual discrimination.

Why is this? Because sentient beings each possess their own wholesome karma from past lives, and the Bodhisattva previously made the vow to deliver sentient beings; by the power of this vow, he manifests transformation bodies according to their thoughts, and thus there is no conceptual discrimination.

These bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), are able to perform such deeds of transforming sentient beings and swiftly proceed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Why is this?

These bodhisattvas have perfected generosity; their ethical discipline is pure, without breach, flaw, or admixture, and their purity of the precepts surpasses that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. They are fully endowed with patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime vows, powers, and knowledge, as well as the unique qualities of the Tathāgatas, because they have transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

“O Heavenly King, you should know that from the first bhūmi through the tenth bhūmi, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and cultivates such conduct, they are able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

When this Dharma was being taught, twenty thousand devaputras were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye; thirty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand devas and humans together resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Countless hundreds of thousands of gandharvas and kinnaras circumambulated Vulture Peak Mountain, joyfully joining their palms in praise of the Tathāgata; countless hundreds of thousands of yakṣas likewise circumambulated Vulture Peak Mountain, joyfully joining their palms and raining down various exquisite flowers as an offering to the Buddha.
From the infinite Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable bodhisattvas each gathered there to offer praise, saying:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has skillfully expounded the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattvas."

It is because of this *prajñāpāramitā* that there exist the four paths and four fruits of humans and devas, as well as the path of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) and their enlightenment; furthermore, the ten stages and ten perfections of the bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—all these boundless Buddha-dharmas are accomplished through the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Just as all worldly phenomena depend upon space, yet space has no dependence;
so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: it is the foundation of all dharmas, yet itself has no dependence.
May we, in future ages, proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, exactly as the World-Honored One has taught it now, without any difference.
Having spoken these words, he took various fragrant flowers and scattered them as an offering over the Tathāgata and the entire assembly.
At that time, immeasurable devas who had long resided on Vulture Peak Mountain and others who had gathered there praised him from mid-air, saying:
"How marvelous! How rare!"
"Bhagavān!
We recall that in the past, immeasurable Buddhas have already expounded the Prajñāpāramitā for the great assemblies here on this Vulture Peak Mountain, no different from what is being done now."
At that time, Jyotiṣprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Do the devas in the sky possess the wisdom to know the distinctions regarding the duration of the Buddha’s realm, such that they could say that immeasurable Buddhas have already taught the Prajñāpāramitā here?"
The Buddha said, “O Heavenly King!

This assembly of devas are all bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation; therefore, they are able to know the distinctions regarding the duration and proximity of the realms of past buddhas.”
"O Devaputra!

In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I was also born among those in the realm of the devas. There, I saw immeasurable Buddhas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they proclaimed the sublime Dharma to the various assemblies until their parinirvāṇa; I constantly paid them homage with palms joined and offered praise."
"Why is this? Because the lifespan of those devas in that celestial realm is exceedingly long, and they have seen and heard of boundless events from the past.

At that time, among the assembly there was a son of heaven named Prabhāśrī. He rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas should dwell in pure lands; why has the World-Honored One appeared here in this Sahā world, which is filled with such defilement and evil?”
The Buddha told Prabhāśrī:
"O Son of Heaven, you should know that wherever the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, dwell is entirely free from impurity; it is itself a land of purity."

Thereupon, by means of his supernormal powers, the Tathāgata caused this trichiliocosm to become as level as the palm of a hand, composed of lapis lazuli, devoid of mountains, hills, mounds, or thorns; everywhere there were heaps of jewels, fragrant flowers, soft grasses, springs, ponds with water of eight virtues, stairways of the seven treasures, and flowering fruits, trees, and shrubs, all of which proclaimed:
"The Bodhisattva’s non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma is free from ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas."
Although there were bodhisattvas coming from the ten directions, they heard no other sounds, but only the constant proclamation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Everywhere there were lotus flowers the size of chariot wheels, adorned with various jewels in blue, red, and white;

within the calyxes of these flowers sat bodhisattvas in the full lotus posture, contemplating the Mahāyāna. They beheld this Tathāgata presiding over a great assembly, teaching the profound Dharma to a multitude of bodhisattvas, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas who offered worship, praise, and reverence.
At that time, having witnessed this event, Prabhāśrī leaped for joy and, praising the Buddha, said:
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One!"
"How rare!
Well-gone One!
