What the Tathāgata has spoken is true and not false; wherever the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, dwell, there is no impurity whatsoever—it is a pure land."
As the Buddha has taught, its meaning is non-dual; yet sentient beings of meager merit perceive what is pure as impure.
World-Honored One!
If good sons and good daughters should hear even the name of the merits of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is truly rare indeed!
"How much more so, then, could one write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, or explain it for others!
The Buddha told Guṇaprabha:
"O Devaputra, you should know this!"
If good sons and good daughters, throughout immeasurable great kalpas, were to give all manner of material wealth to sentient beings with an unobstructed mind;

yet another good son or good daughter were to, with pure faith, transcribe this sutra and further bestow it upon others for them to accept, uphold, read, and recite—the merit obtained by the latter would far exceed that of the former.
Why is this? Material giving is exhaustible, while the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible. Why is this?

The gift of material wealth can only yield worldly fruits; the fruits of pleasure among humans and devas, though once attained, are lost again. Although they may be obtained for a time now, one will inevitably fall away from them later.
If, however, one gives the gift of Dharma, one attains what was never before attained—namely, Nirvana—which by its very nature is free from the possibility of decline.
"Suppose there were someone who taught and transformed all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm, causing them all to abide securely in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Yet, if a son or daughter of good family, with pure faith, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this profound Prajñāpāramitā to others, their merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and boundless degree."
Why is this? Because all wholesome dharmas arise from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Suppose there were someone who taught and transformed the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm, causing them all to realize the four stages of approach and the four fruits of arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
If good sons or good daughters, with pure faith, uphold, recite, and transcribe this Prajñāpāramitā, their merit will surpass the former by immeasurable and incalculable degrees.
Why is this? Because both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
All the dharmas of the bodhisattvas appear from the perfection of wisdom; it is because of this perfection of wisdom that Buddhas appear in the world.
Therefore, wherever the Prajñāpāramitā is present, one should know that it is the sublime seat of enlightenment and also the place where the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma.
"Sons of good family!
You should maintain the mindfulness that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is always present in this place. Why is this?"
Because all Buddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
the merit obtained by one who makes offerings to an image of the Tathāgata is not equal to that obtained by making offerings to the profound perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? It is because all Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained their existence by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 569, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Seven: On Equality (*Samatā-varga*) At that time, the Most Excellent One rose again from his seat, draped his upper robe over his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has taught that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal, what is meant by ‘equality’?
By being equal to what phenomena is it called ‘equal’?
The Buddha told Sujaya:
“O Heavenly King, you should know!
Because one observes all phenomena as being quiescent in their intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing, they are called ‘equality.
Because all afflictions and false conceptualizations are quiescent in their intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing, they are called ‘equality.’”
The self-nature of the discrimination of names and signs is quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing; therefore, it is called equality.
All perversions are extinguished and no further攀緣 (pāra-ālambana, objective clinging) arises; therefore, it is called equality.

The mind that acts as the subject of cognition is extinguished, and ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) are both simultaneously quiescent; because delusion and craving have been extinguished, one no longer clings to "I" and "mine"; therefore, it is called equality.
Because the grasping at "self" and "mine" has been forever extinguished, name-and-form are tranquil; therefore, they are called equanimity.
Because name-and-form have ceased, extreme views do not arise; therefore, they are called equanimity.
Because the views of annihilation and permanence have been extinguished, the view of a self-identity is tranquil; therefore, they are called equanimity.
"O Devaputra, you should know!

All afflictions that obstruct wholesome dharmas—both the grasper and the grasped—arise based on the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they can extinguish this view of a self-entity; then all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and all afflictions will be forever stilled, and even their formative aspirations (*praṇidhāna*) will cease."
It is like a great tree whose roots and stumps have been uprooted; its branches, twigs, and leaves will all wither and die.
It is like a person without a head, whose life-force and other vital functions are severed.
The latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are likewise: if the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, all others are eternally extinguished.
If a person can contemplate that all phenomena are without self, both the grasper and the grasped are eternally stilled.
At that time, Ajita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way does the view of self obstruct the true principle?
The Buddha told Ajita:
"O Deva, you should know this!

To falsely claim a self within the five aggregates of clinging gives rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The true Dharma is equal in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), devoid of both subject and object of grasping; since the view of a self is contrary to this, it constitutes an obstruction."
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
This view of self does not exist within, nor without, nor in between; being entirely without abode, it is called 'quiescence,' which is itself equanimity.
To be far removed from the view of self and to penetrate equanimity is called 'true emptiness.'"

Observing this emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—its self-nature being quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, neither grasped nor attached, and far removed from the view of a self—it is therefore called equality.
"O Heavenly King, you should know that what is called 'self' neither comes nor goes; it lacks any reality and is a false discrimination. Phenomena arise from delusion and are themselves illusory."
If bodhisattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, contemplate these dharmas as being far removed from falsehood, this is therefore called "quiescent equality."
"O Heavenly King, you should know that the grasper and the grasped are called 'blazing'; their transcendence is called 'quiescence.
All afflictive obstructions are called 'blazing'; their transcendence is called 'quiescence.'"

If Bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they are able to know, as it truly is, that the cessation of the grasping subject and the grasped object—the various afflictions—is an increasing wholesome dharma; by severing both the grasping subject and object as well as the afflictions, they see nothing that can arise and see nothing that can cease, and thus it is called "equality.

By cultivating all types of *pāramitās* while remaining far removed from demonic obstacles, they see nothing that can be cultivated and see nothing that can be abandoned, and thus it is called "equality."

A bodhisattva constantly takes the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) as their object and does not give rise to the mental orientations (manasikāra) of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; because they do not perceive any difference between the factors of enlightenment and those of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it is called "equality.

Taking all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) as their object, their minds never rest as they constantly cultivate the practice of emptiness (śūnyatā); yet, by the power of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), they do not abandon sentient beings—therefore, it is called "equality."
“O Heavenly King, you should know this!
If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), their minds attain mastery over all phenomena as objects of focus;
they cultivate awakening by focusing on the signless (*animitta*), yet they do not perceive any difference between the signless and awakening—therefore, it is called ‘equality.’”
The mind takes non-aspiration as its object yet does not abandon the triple world; it perceives no difference between non-aspiration and the triple world, and is thus called "equality.
It contemplates the impurity of the body while the mind abides in purity;
it contemplates the impermanence of conditioned phenomena while the mind takes birth and death as its object without weariness or renunciation.
Contemplating the suffering of sentient beings, they abide in the bliss of nirvana;

contemplating the selflessness of phenomena, they give rise to great compassion for all classes of sentient beings. They constantly preach the medicine of impurity to sentient beings, yet do not perceive the disease of greed;
they constantly preach great loving-kindness, yet do not perceive the disease of hatred.
He constantly teaches dependent origination and does not perceive the disease of ignorance;
for those with the disease of equality, he prescribes the medicine of impermanence, yet he does not perceive the disease of equality as distinct from impermanence.
Thus, the bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means possesses sovereign mastery over the mind regarding all phenomena.
Taking as their object the dharma of freedom from greed, they transform śrāvakas;
taking as their object the dharma of freedom from hatred, they transform pratyekabuddhas;
taking as their object the dharma of freedom from delusion, they transform bodhisattvas.
Contemplating all forms, they vow to attain the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous form, yet do so without apprehending anything;
contemplating all sounds, they do so for the sake of attaining the subtle and wonderful voices of all Buddhas, yet do so without apprehending anything;
contemplating all fragrances, they vow to attain the pure fragrance of the precepts of all Buddhas, yet do so without apprehending anything.
Contemplating all tastes, he vows to attain the Tathāgata’s mark of being the foremost among great men regarding taste, because of non-apprehension;
contemplating all tangibles, he vows to attain the Tathāgata’s soft palms, because of non-apprehension;
contemplating all phenomena, he vows to attain the Tathāgata’s tranquil mind, because of non-apprehension.
Relying on all acts of giving, they seek to achieve the body adorned with the marks and signs of a Buddha;
relying on all pure precepts, they seek to attain a perfectly adorned and purified Buddha-field;
relying on all forms of patience, they vow to obtain the great Brahma-voice of all Buddhas and the pure radiant bodies of all Buddhas.
They rely on all forms of diligence to continuously deliver sentient beings without interruption;
they rely on all forms of meditative concentration to achieve vast supernormal powers;
and they rely on all forms of wisdom to sever all deluded views and afflictions.
By means of great loving-kindness that is impartial and unimpeded, they bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
by means of great compassion, they protect the true Dharma and rescue sentient beings from the great suffering of birth and death;
by means of great sympathetic joy, they attain unhindered mastery in preaching the Dharma to delight and gladden sentient beings.
“By relying on great equanimity, one does not grasp at the afflictions, fetters, bonds, or latent tendencies of sentient beings who hold views.
‘O Heavenly King, you should know that if bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they do not perceive two things; this is called practicing equanimity.’”
Taking the four means of attraction as the object of focus, one acts to transform sentient beings;
taking the faults of stinginess and envy as the object of focus, one relinquishes material resources to practice generosity;
and taking the failure of precept-keeping as the object of focus, one abides in pure morality.
To remedy the loss caused by anger and resentment, one practices patience;
to remedy the loss caused by indolence, one accomplishes the Tathāgata’s power of great diligence;
and to remedy the loss caused by distraction, one attains the Tathāgata’s supreme meditative concentration of tranquility.
Taking the loss of impaired wisdom as a condition, it is for the sake of accomplishing the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom;
taking the Dharma of the Two Vehicles as a condition, it is because of the desire to accomplish the unsurpassed Mahāyāna;
and taking the various evil destinies as a condition, it is because of the desire to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
He takes the various happy realms as his object in order to cause [beings] to know that the fruits of human and celestial existence are all destined to perish;
he takes all sentient beings as his object in order to lead them to realize that there is nothing substantial therein, only falsehood;
and he takes the recollection of the Buddha as his object in order to achieve the superior concentrations that assist the path.
One contemplates the recollection of the Dharma in order to attain penetration into the secret treasury of all dharmas;
one contemplates the recollection of the Saṃgha so that the minds of the harmonious assembly may be without regression;
and one contemplates the recollection of relinquishment so as to be free from attachment.
One contemplates the recollection of the precepts (*śīlānusmṛti*) in order to attain pure ethical discipline;
one contemplates the recollection of the devas (*devatānusmṛti*) in order to achieve the praise of the various devas for one's bodhi;
and one contemplates the marks of one's own body (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*) in order to attain the Buddha-body.
By taking the characteristics of one's own words as the object of focus, one attains the speech of the Buddha;
by taking the characteristics of one's own mind as the object of focus, one attains the equanimous mind of all Buddhas;

by taking conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as the object of focus, one accomplishes the wisdom of a Buddha; and by taking unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) as the object of focus, one attains tranquility.
“O Heavenly King, you should know this!

If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), there is not a single thought or a single action that passes in vain without being dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).”
In this way, a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, although universally taking all phenomena as objects of cognition, remains unattached to them;
therefore, it is called "skillful means observing all phenomena such that none do not tend toward great enlightenment."
"Just as all things produced within the trichiliocosm are for the enjoyment of sentient beings, so too,

there is no object of focus or sphere of activity for a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means that does not benefit those who are advancing toward enlightenment."
Just as there are no visible forms that do not depend upon the four great elements, so too,
among all phenomena that serve as the objects of a bodhisattva’s focus, there is not a single dharma that does not tend toward enlightenment.

Why is this? The practice of bodhisattvas is established entirely through external conditions; that is to say, it is by reason of those who are stingy and envious that bodhisattvas accomplish the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), and by reason of those who are ungrateful that they accomplish the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
For those with a malicious nature, they accomplish the perfection of patience;
for those who are indolent, they accomplish the perfection of diligence;
for those who are distracted, they accomplish the perfection of meditative concentration.
Those who are deluded bring about the perfection of wisdom;
if sentient beings cause harm or affliction to a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva, because of them, subdues and eliminates anger.
"If a bodhisattva sees one practicing wholesome dharmas directed toward enlightenment, they conceive the thought of that person as their own child.
Thus, the bodhisattva does not give rise to joy when praised, nor do they give rise to anger when reviled;
seeing those who lack happiness, they arouse a mind of great compassion."
Seeing those who suffer, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion;
seeing those who possess happiness, one gives rise to the mind of great sympathetic joy;
seeing those who are free from suffering, one gives rise to the mind of great equanimity.
For those who are difficult to transform, one arouses *śamatha*;
for those who are easy to transform, one arouses *vipaśyanā*;
and for those who practice by way of faith, one gives rise to the wisdom that recognizes kindness.
If one perceives that external adverse conditions prevail over external favorable conditions for sentient beings, one diligently protects them;
if one perceives that the power of their causes is strong and superior, one employs various skillful means to cause them to receive the teachings;
and if one perceives that sentient beings have attained awakening through wisdom, one then proclaims for them the essential points of the profound Dharma.
If one perceives that sentient beings will only attain awakening through extensive exposition, then one teaches the various dharmas in successive order;
if sentient beings are attached to the literal words, one explains the meaning of the phrases to bring them to understanding;
and if they have already trained in śamatha, one teaches them sublime vipaśyanā.
If one has already studied contemplation, one teaches them tranquil cessation (śamatha);
if one clings to the precepts, one speaks of the hells;
if one upholds the precepts without clinging, one does not speak of them.
If they cling to the wisdom of hearing, he teaches them the wisdom of reflection and cultivation;
if they cling to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he teaches them *prajñā*;
and if there are those who delight in forest retreats (*āraṇyaka*), he teaches them the Dharma of mental seclusion.
If there are those who delight in hearing of the Buddha’s merits, he teaches them the unsurpassed noble wisdom;
for those with lustful desires, he teaches the dharma of impurity;
for those with anger and hatred, he teaches the dharma of loving-kindness and compassion.
For those who are deluded, he teaches the Dharma of dependent origination;
for those with equal proportions of the defilements, he teaches various dharmas—sometimes teaching on impurity, sometimes on loving-kindness and compassion, and sometimes on dependent origination;
and for those already disciplined, he teaches pure precepts, supreme concentration, and sublime wisdom.
For those who should enter the Buddha Vehicle and be transformed, he teaches the *pāramitās* in successive order;
for those who should be transformed through suppression, he first refutes their arguments and subsequently preaches the Dharma;
for those who should be transformed through various modes of speech, he immediately explains to them through causes, conditions, and parables so that they may attain understanding.
For those who should be transformed by means of the profound Dharma, one teaches the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*—selflessness and the non-existence of phenomena;
for those attached to various views, one teaches the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
and for those with excessive discursive thought and investigation, one teaches signlessness (*animitta*).
For those attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), he teaches wishlessness (*apraṇihita*);
for those attached to the aggregates (*skandha*), he teaches that they are like illusions;
for those attached to the elements (*dhātu*), he teaches the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
For those attached to the various sense bases, he teaches that they are like dreams;
for those attached to the desire realm, he teaches that it is ablaze;
for those attached to the form realm, he teaches that it is characterized by the suffering of conditioned existence.
For those attached to the formless realm, he teaches that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
for sentient beings who are difficult to transform, he praises the noble lineages;
for sentient beings who are easy to transform, he teaches the meditative absorptions and the immeasurable minds.
If those who hear [the teaching] are transformed by the thought of being reborn in heaven, he speaks of happiness;
if they are transformed by means of the Śrāvaka-dharma, he speaks of the Noble Truths;
if they are transformed by means of the Pratyekabuddha-dharma, he speaks of dependent origination.
For those who are transformed by means of the Bodhisattva-dharma, he preaches the dharma of the pure mind and great compassion;
for those practicing as Bodhisattvas, he preaches merit and wisdom;
for non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, he preaches the Pure Land.
For bodhisattvas bound to one more birth, he explains the adornment of the Bodhi seat;
for those who are to be transformed by the Buddha’s teaching, he speaks to them according to the continuous sequence of their spiritual progression.

"O Heavenly King, you should know that when a bodhisattva thus practices the pure and profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they attain all forms of mastery through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and their teaching of the Dharma for the benefit of others is never in vain."

When this Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s mastery was being taught, thirty thousand devas and humans simultaneously gave rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and five thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.

It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they manifest a smile, various colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal-clear—issue forth from the gateway of their face, universally illuminating the boundless worlds of the ten directions. Having manifested this rare event, the light returns to the Buddha’s presence, circumambulates him three times to the right, and enters the crown of his head.

At that time, Śāriputra, beholding this auspicious sign, felt a sense of hesitation in his heart. He immediately rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"For what cause and condition has this auspicious sign appeared?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"This Most Victorious Deva, in the past, throughout immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great kalpas, practiced all the pāramitās in the presence of various Buddhas and served as a guardian of the prajñāpāramitā for all bodhisattvas. By virtue of these causes and conditions, he has now encountered me and is able to receive instruction on the prajñāpāramitā."

In future ages, after further passing through immeasurable and incalculable great kalpas, he will cultivate the provisions for unsurpassed bodhi; thereafter, he will realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment he seeks, becoming endowed with the ten titles. His Buddha-name will be Guṇavyūha (Adorned with Virtue), his land will be named Parama-vyūha-viśuddha (Utmost Adornment and Purity), and the kalpa will be named Viśuddha (Pure).
“That land is prosperous and joyful, with a vast and flourishing population; it consists solely of a community of bodhisattvas, with no śrāvakas.

The great earth of that land is composed of the seven treasures, adorned with various jewels and as level as the palm of a hand. It is embellished with fragrant flowers and soft grasses, and is free from mountains, hills, mounds, or thorns, being further adorned with various banners, streamers, and flower canopies.”

There was a great capital city named Invincible (*Durjayā*), its surface completely covered by nets of the seven treasures. Golden cords crisscrossed it, with golden bells suspended at the corners; throughout the six periods of day and night, celestial music resounded from the sky, and various kinds of exquisite celestial incense and flowers were scattered.
The inhabitants of that land enjoy themselves with joy and pleasure, surpassing even the exquisite splendors of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
humans and devas come and go without obstruction, and there are no names for the three evil realms or the two vehicles.
The sentient beings of that land seek only the wisdom of a Buddha, and that Buddha constantly proclaims various essential teachings of purity for the sake of the great bodhisattvas.

His immeasurable and boundless assembly of bodhisattva followers is free from wrong views and attachments, broken precepts, and wrong livelihoods; nor do they suffer from blindness, deafness, muteness, hunchback, or any other physical defects or unwholesome conditions, their bodies being adorned with the twenty-eight marks of excellence.
The Tathāgata of that land has a lifespan of eight minor kalpas, and among the hosts of humans and devas, none suffer premature death.

The Buddha possesses such immeasurable merit that when he wishes to preach the Dharma, he first emits a radiance; once the assembly of bodhisattvas encounters this light, they immediately know that the World-Honored One is about to preach the Dharma and think, "We should now go to listen."
At that time, the devas prepared a lion throne for the Buddha, measuring one hundred yojanas in height and breadth, adorned with various ornaments and presented with immeasurable offerings.

The World-Honored One ascended the throne and preached the Dharma for the assembly. Those bodhisattvas were intelligent and of sharp faculties; upon hearing it once, they attained realization, becoming free from the notions of "self" and "mine. All necessary requisites and food and drink arrived as soon as they were thought of.

When the Buddha spoke this Dharma of the Prediction of Supreme Attainment, fifty thousand devas and humans were filled with profound joy; they all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, each vowing to be born in that buddha-field in the future.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Suvikrānta was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented occurrence; he ascended into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees.

At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the celestial musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, as they scattered various heavenly flowers as an offering to the Buddha, the great bodhisattvas, and King Suvikrānta.
Then, that celestial king descended from the sky, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Chapter 6: Manifesting Signs, Part 8. At that time, Śāriputra asked the Most Victorious One:

“When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he should at that very moment sit upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings. For what reason does he first manifest six years of asceticism, subdue the celestial Māra, and only afterwards achieve perfect awakening?”
The Most Victorious One replied: "Virtuous One, you should know!

When a Bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they master the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). In reality, there are no ascetic practices; these are manifested only to subdue those of external paths. Furthermore, that celestial Māra is the lord of the desire realm; by his very nature he is disciplined and gentle, and thus truly should not be destroyed. Yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he is shown to be subdued."

It refers to those non-Buddhists who claim to be foremost in the practice of asceticism; therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests the ability to practice asceticism that surpasses theirs— namely, some sentient beings may see the Bodhisattva standing with one knee bent,
or see him standing with both hands raised,
or see him standing while gazing at the sun.
Some see the Bodhisattva scorching his body with the five heats;
some see the Bodhisattva hanging upside down;
some see the Bodhisattva lying upon thorns, or lying on cow dung, or sitting upon a stone, or again lying on the ground, or lying on a wooden board, or lying on a pestle, or lying in ashes and dust.

In some instances, one sees the Bodhisattva wearing only wooden plank robes, or robes of *māñjiṣṭha* grass, or robes of grass, or robes of tree bark, or robes of reeds; or again, he is seen naked, or facing the sun and turning with it as it moves.

In other instances, one sees the Bodhisattva eating only millet, or eating wheat, or eating grass roots, or eating tree leaves, or flowers, or fruits; or eating yams, or taro, or lotus roots, or beans, or grains, or hemp, or rice; or eating once every six days, or passing the days by drinking only water; or on a single day consuming a single drop of clarified butter, or a single drop of honey, or a single drop of milk; or eating nothing at all, or remaining in constant deep sleep.
He manifested various such ascetic practices for six years without a single lapse;
yet in reality, the Bodhisattva had no such asceticism, but rather, while he was capable of liberating sentient beings, he perceived himself as a Bodhisattva manifesting such asceticism.
At that time, there were sixty nayutas of devas and humans who, upon witnessing this event, became established in the Three Vehicles.

Furthermore, there were devas and humans whose power of past roots of goodness led them to deeply delight in the Mahāyāna; they saw the Bodhisattva seated upon a pedestal of the seven precious gems, his body and mind unmoving, his face serene with a smile as he entered a supreme samādhi, from which he would only arise after six years had passed.

There were also multitudes of devas and humans who deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna and desired to hear the teaching; they saw the Bodhisattva sitting upright, preaching the Dharma for the duration of six years.

"Venerable One, you should know that this Bodhisattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), was able to subdue the celestial Māras and overcome all non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*). Out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he transformed and delivered all sentient beings. Having completed six years, he arose from his meditative absorption and, in accordance with worldly custom, went to the River Nairañjanā; having bathed and emerged, he stood upon the riverbank."
There was a cowherd girl who milked one hundred cows to feed a single cow, and having drawn the milk from this cow, she prepared a milk porridge to offer to the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, six hundred million devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others each brought various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink to present as offerings, all saying:
"O Great Being!..."
"O Noble One!
I pray that you will accept my offering of food and drink.
The Bodhisattva, out of compassion for them, accepted it all.
At that time, the cowherd girl, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others could not see one another; each saw only the Bodhisattva alone receiving their offerings.

At that time, there were immeasurable devas, humans, and others who, upon seeing him receive offerings, all attained realization of the Way; for this reason, the Bodhisattva manifested such an appearance.
In reality, at that time, the Bodhisattva did not actually bathe, nor did he truly accept the offerings from those humans, devas, and others.

"Venerable Sir, you should know that it is through such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that a bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* manifests the act of proceeding to the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."

At that time, there was a terrestrial deity named Wonderful Ground (Sudhara), who, together with a host of celestial beings, swept and adorned the area on all sides, sprinkled it with scented water, and scattered wonderful flowers.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings of this trichiliocosm, leading their respective celestial hosts, rained down exquisite celestial flowers as an offering to the Bodhisattva.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Heavenly King Kāla, leading their respective celestial hosts, remained in mid-air playing celestial music and praising the Bodhisattva.

The Heavenly King Nirmāṇarati, leading his own celestial host, held a net of the seven treasures that completely covered the world; from the four corners of this net hung bells of purple gold, all raining down various jewels as an offering to the Bodhisattva.

The Heavenly King Śubhavimāna led his own celestial host, holding a net of purple-gold that completely covered the world; they performed various celestial music and rained down all kinds of flowers as an offering to the Bodhisattva.

The Lord of the Heaven of Sovereign Power (*Īśāna*), leading his own celestial host, along with the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, each held various kinds of exquisite offerings to pay homage to the Bodhisattva.
When Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, saw that the Bodhisattva had approached the seat of enlightenment, he immediately addressed the entire assembly of Brahmās, saying:
"You should all know this!"
Now this bodhisattva has adorned himself with firm armor; he does not violate his original vow and his mind is free from weariness or indolence.

He has fulfilled all the practices of a bodhisattva, attained mastery over the teachings for the infinite transformation of sentient beings, gained sovereign power over all the bodhisattva stages, and possesses a pure mind toward all sentient beings, being well-versed in [their needs].
He thoroughly penetrates the distinctions among all faculties and natures, realizes the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, and transcends all the activities of Māra.

He accumulates the roots of all virtues without depending on external conditions, is protected and mindful of by all Tathāgatas, and universally opens the gate of liberation for all sentient beings. As a great general and guide, he crushes the enemy forces of Māra.
Uniquely renowned as courageous throughout the great trichiliocosm, he is a great King of Physicians who skillfully bestows the medicine of the Dharma;

having received the empowerment of liberation, he has ascended to the rank of Dharma King; emitting the light of wisdom that universally illumines all, he remains unstained by the eight worldly concerns like a lotus flower;
he has attained unimpeded mastery over all gateways of dhāraṇī; his depth and breadth are unfathomable, like...
Like the great ocean, he is stable and immovable as Mount Sumeru; his wisdom is pure and free from all defilement and turbidity;
he is radiant within and without like a mani jewel; he has attained mastery over the characteristics of all phenomena;
and his holy life is pristine, having reached its ultimate consummation.

Thus, the bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means proceeds to the seat of awakening (*bodhimanda*) to deliver sentient beings; there, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he subdues the hosts of Māra. To accomplish the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as other immeasurable and boundless buddha-qualities, he turns the great wheel of Dharma and utters the lion’s roar. He universally bestows the Dharma upon all sentient beings, satisfying each according to their needs and capacities. To purify the Dharma-eye for all sentient beings and to subdue the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) with the unsurpassed Dharma, he desires to demonstrate the fulfillment of the original vows of all Buddhas, attaining mastery over all phenomena.
"You all should go and make offerings to the Bodhisattva.

"Venerable ones, you should know that it is through such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that this Bodhisattva manifests the act of proceeding to the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."

At that time, from the marks of the thousand-spoked wheels on his two soles, immeasurable and subtle rays of light were emitted, universally illuminating the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; all sentient beings therein who encountered this light immediately became free from suffering, their bodies and minds at peace and joyful.
At that time, within the dragon palace, there was a great dragon king named Karika. Having encountered this light, he gave rise to great joy and addressed the dragons, saying:
"This wondrous radiance has come to illuminate us, bringing peace and happiness to our bodies and minds."

"In the past, I once beheld this light when a Tathāgata appeared in the world; now that there is this subtle and wondrous radiance, I know for certain that a Buddha has appeared in the world. We should together prepare various fragrant flowers, diverse and exquisite treasures, banners, streamers, and flower-canopies, and go to offer worship accompanied by all manner of musical performances."

Thereupon, the Dragon King, together with his retinue, brought forth offerings and extensively raised a great cloud that rained down fragrant showers. He went before the Bodhisattva, performed various musical concerts, and made offerings; circumambulating the Bodhisattva to the right, he praised him, saying:
"This subtle and wondrous radiance brings universal joy; there is no doubt that the most supreme Buddha will certainly appear.

All manner of rare treasures adorn the great earth, and the grasses and trees that grow there have all been transformed into jewels. The rivers and streams are all stilled, free from the sound of wind and waves; by these signs, we know for certain that a Buddha has appeared in the world."
The radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, the sun, and the moon does not appear; the evil realms become purified—there is no doubt that a Buddha has appeared.
Just as when someone who lost his parents in youth suddenly regains them upon reaching adulthood, he leaps for joy, unable to contain himself;
so too do all those in the world rejoice when they behold the appearance of a Buddha.
"We have made offerings to various Buddhas in the past; now that we have encountered the Dharma King, the Lion among Men, our lives have not been lived in vain.
"Virtuous One, you should know this!"

In this way, the bodhisattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, accepted the grass to spread as a seat beneath the Bodhi tree, circumambulated it seven times to the right, and sat down upright with correct mindfulness.
While inferior sentient beings perceive such signs, the great bodhisattvas see eighty-four thousand devaputras each separately arranging a great lion throne.

The various lion thrones were composed of many jewels, with nets of the seven precious substances spread over them; exquisite golden bells were suspended from each of the four corners, and banners, streamers, and silk canopies were arrayed everywhere.
The Bodhisattva sat cross-legged upon each of these eighty-four thousand lion thrones; yet the sons of the gods did not see one another, and each thought:
"The Bodhisattva is sitting alone on my throne, having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“By these causes and conditions, they give rise to profound joy and all attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed enlightenment.

‘Virtuous One, you should know that when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), the tuft of hair between his eyebrows emits a great radiance that universally illumines the trichiliocosm, causing all the palaces of Māra to lose their majestic splendor.’”
At that time, all the Māra kings thought to themselves:

"For what reason does this radiance appear, eclipsing our own majestic light and our palaces? Could it not be that the Bodhisattva is seated upon the seat of enlightenment, about to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?"
Having thought thus, they looked together and finally saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the Bodhi tree upon the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*).

Upon seeing him, they were struck with terror and summoned the demonic armies—countless hundreds of thousands of diverse forms, bearing various musical instruments, various banners and streamers, and emitting various sounds that caused blood to flow from every orifice and pore of those who heard them.

At that time, by the power of great compassion, the Bodhisattva causes the hosts of Māra’s army to be unable to utter a sound; this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means in practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

“Venerable Sir, you should know that a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means recollects past immeasurable billions of eons, having fully perfected the diligent cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the branches of the path, tranquility, insight, the three types of higher knowledge, and the eight liberations.”
Having reflected thus, he immediately extended his golden right hand, stroking from the crown of his head down through his entire body, and spoke these words:
"I wish to deliver sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and give rise to great compassion."
At that time, when the various Māra kings and their retinues heard the Bodhisattva’s words, they all fell prostrate.
Then, by the power of his great compassion, the Bodhisattva caused the hosts of Māras to hear a voice from the air:
"You should take refuge in the Great Seer of Pure Precepts, who bestows fearlessness and protects all beings."
When Māra and his retinue heard these words, they remained prostrate on the ground and spoke thus:
"We pray only that the Great Seer will save our lives.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, relying on the skillful means of profound *prajñāpāramitā*, emitted a great radiance; all who encountered it were freed from fear.
When Māra and his retinue beheld this supernatural manifestation, fear and joy were simultaneously stirred within them.
"Virtuous One, you should know that such a bodhisattva,
practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), causes sentient beings to perceive things differently, namely:
Some see him thus subduing Māra, while other sentient beings do not see this event;
some see the Bodhisattva seated merely upon a grass mat,
while others see him dwelling upon a lion throne.
Some see the Bodhisattva sitting on the ground;
others see him sitting upon a lion throne in mid-air.
They see the Bodhi tree in various forms as well, such as seeing it as a pāṭala tree.
Some see this as a celestial tree of variegated colors;
some see this tree as composed of various jewels;
some see this tree as being seven *tāla* trees in height.
Some see this tree measuring eighty-four thousand yojanas, with a lion throne measuring forty-two thousand yojanas beneath it, where the Bodhisattva sits;
some see the Bodhisattva sporting in mid-air;
or some see him seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
In this way, the bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means manifests various supernatural transformations to deliver all sentient beings.
“Virtuous One, you should know this:

when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means and sits upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless—from each of the ten directions all gather there. Abiding in the midst of space, they utter various sounds to comfort the bodhisattva, causing his body to be at ease and his mind to feel joy, saying:
‘Excellent!’”
"O Mahāsattva!

With courageous diligence, you shall swiftly accomplish vast and auspicious merit. Let your mind be like a vajra and do not give rise to fear; sporting with supernatural powers for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, you will be able to realize all-knowledge in a single kṣaṇa."

"In this way, when a bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, even if Māra comes to disturb and confuse him, he does not give rise to anger at all. With a single moment of mind, through skillful means, he is able to accord with the principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, having reached the ultimate and attained thorough penetration of all that is to be known, seen, and realized."

“Venerable One, you should know that when a bodhisattva who practices the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means sits upon the seat of enlightenment, all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions— as many as there are worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— will, with one voice,
praise him, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
Excellent, Great Being!
You are indeed able to penetrate spontaneous wisdom, unimpeded wisdom, impartial wisdom, and teacherless wisdom, adorned with great compassion.
"Venerable sir, you should know that when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they are able to manifest such various displays."

Among the various classes of sentient beings, some see the Bodhisattva attaining awakening now, while others see him having already attained Buddhahood long ago. Some see only the four Great Heavenly Kings of a single world-system each offering a bowl, while others see the four Great Heavenly Kings from as many world-systems in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, each offering a bowl. At that time, for the sake of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva accepts all these bowls together, stacking them in his palms and pressing them with his hand so that they merge into one.
The four Great Heavenly Kings do not see one another, and each thinks, "The World-Honored One has accepted my bowl alone."
At that time, sixty thousand devaputras, impelled by the power of their past vows, arrived first to present offerings. In the past, they had made this vow, saying:
"When this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, may we receive his very first offering."

When this Dharma was being taught, thirty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); furthermore, thirty-six thousand bodhisattvas all attained the stage of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Eighty thousand humans and devas became free from dust and defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), while immeasurable and boundless sentient beings all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Venerable sir, you should know that at that time,
the Bodhisattva, relying on the skillful means of profound prajñāpāramitā, was about to manifest the turning of the great wheel of Dharma."

The Lord of the Sahā World, the Brahma King Śikhin, together with an assembly of six million eight hundred thousand Brahmās, immediately came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and made this request three times:
"We pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on us and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma!"
"Only we pray that you, out of great compassion, take pity on us and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma!
Only we pray that you, out of great compassion, take pity on us and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma!
Having made this request three times, he immediately manifested a great lion throne; the throne was forty-two thousand yojanas in height and breadth, adorned in various ways, firm, and secure.

At that time, in each of the worlds of the ten directions, there were immeasurable Indras, lords of the devas, who all prepared lion thrones for the Tathāgata; their dimensions and adornments were likewise as described.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested supernatural powers, causing each of those devas to see the Bodhisattva sitting upon his seat and turning the wheel of Dharma.

Once the Bodhisattva was seated upon this lion throne, he entered the samādhi-door of the boundless realm and emitted a great radiance that illuminated worlds in the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

Furthermore, he causes that realm to undergo six kinds of transformations; therein, the manifold sufferings of sentient beings are momentarily stilled, their bodies and minds become peaceful and blissful, and they also temporarily distance themselves from unwholesome and evil states such as greed, hatred, and delusion, regarding one another with loving-kindness like a mother and her child.

At that time, this trichiliocosm was so completely filled by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans that there was not even an interval the size of a single pore.

If there are sentient beings who should be transformed by hearing the teaching on suffering, they hear the Buddha speak of suffering; likewise, those who should be transformed by hearing the teachings on selflessness, tranquility, detachment, impermanence, and emptiness do so as well.

Those who should be transformed by hearing that things are like illusions hear the teaching on being like illusions; likewise, those who should be transformed by hearing that things are like dreams, echoes, reflections, shadows, mirages, transformations, or cities of Gandharvas do so as well.
Those who should be transformed by hearing the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—hear the Buddha speak of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

At that time, among the classes of sentient beings, some heard the Tathāgata teach that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; some heard him teach the aggregates (*skandha*); some heard him teach the elements (*dhātu*); some heard him teach the sense bases (*āyatana*); some heard him teach suffering (*duḥkha*), some the origin (*samudaya*), some cessation (*nirodha*), and some the path (*mārga*). Some heard him teach the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the branches of the path. Some heard him teach calm abiding (*śamatha*) and special insight (*vipaśyanā*). Some heard him teach the various dharmas of the śrāvakas, some the various dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and some the various dharmas of the bodhisattvas.

"In this way, the bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means manifests various signs of turning the wheel of Dharma; according to the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings, each gains benefit and happiness, and their hearts rejoice deeply."
At that time, Śāriputra said to Jyotiṣprabha: “O Devaputra!

When a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, all their spheres of activity are extremely deep, inconceivable, ineffable, difficult to know, and difficult to enter.”
The Most Victorious One replied:
"Virtuous One!
The merits and supreme qualities of a bodhisattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) are immeasurable and boundless."
Of what I have now spoken, not even one part in a hundred, nor one in a thousand, nor even one in a *upaniṣad*-fraction can be found; only the Tathāgata is able to explain it in its entirety.
That which I have now spoken is but a small portion, all of it received through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable; even the assembly of Bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth cannot exhaustively describe its merits, let alone other Bodhisattvas!
"Venerable sir, you should know that the realm of the Buddhas is tranquil and beyond verbal expression; it can be realized only by non-conceptual wisdom and the subsequently attained wisdom.
Venerable sir, you should know this!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize and enter the domain of all Buddhas,
they should study the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* to ultimately penetrate the *vikrāntagāminī-samādhi*,
the *māyopama-samādhi*, the *vajropama-samādhi*, the *vajramaṇḍala-samādhi*, and the *aniñjya-samādhi*.
The samādhi of wisdom, the samādhi of universal penetration, the samādhi of non-referential objects,
the samādhi of lion-like mastery, the samādhi of the king of samādhis,
the samādhi of the adornment of merit, the samādhi of tranquil wisdom, the samādhi of universal transcendence, and the samādhi of non-defilement.
The Samādhi of Adornment, the Samādhi of the King Adorned with Wisdom, the Peerless Samādhi, the Samādhi of Equal Awakening,
the Samādhi of Perfect Awakening, the Pleasing Samādhi, the Joyful Samādhi,
the Pure Samādhi, the Flame Samādhi, and the Radiance Samādhi.
The earth-like samādhi, the difficult-to-conquer samādhi, the ever-present samādhi, the non-combined samādhi,
the unborn samādhi, the penetrating samādhi, the most excellent samādhi,
the samādhi that transcends the realm of Māra, the samādhi of all-knowledge, and the banner-mark samādhi.
The Earth Samādhi, the Great Compassion Samādhi, the Bliss Samādhi, the Affectionate Regard Samādhi,
the Non-Perception of Phenomena Samādhi,
and so forth. "Venerable One, you should know this!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to train in the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will be able to ultimately penetrate these immeasurable and boundless samādhi-gates, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges; they will then be able to enter the realm of all Buddhas, their minds peaceful and secure, free from fear, like a lion king who has no dread of birds or beasts.
Why is this? Because if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates such samādhis as these, whatever they do, they are entirely without fear and perceive no enemy before them.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, their minds have no object of focus and no place of abiding.

For example, suppose there were a person born in the formless realm who, for eighty thousand great kalpas, possesses only a single consciousness that has neither a dwelling place nor an object of perception;
in this same way, a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means has a mind that has neither an object of perception nor a dwelling place.

Why is this? These bodhisattvas do not direct their minds toward the state of non-practice; they do not conceive thoughts regarding the state of non-conception; they do not take objects within the state of non-objectification; they do not cling within the state of non-attachment; their minds are not distracted within the state of non-distraction; their minds have no high or low; their minds have neither opposition nor compliance, neither sorrow nor joy, neither discrimination nor the departure from discrimination, and they are free from both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Their minds do not follow after wisdom, nor do they abide in themselves or in others. They do not abide dependent on the eye, nor do they abide dependent on the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. They do not abide dependent on forms, nor do they abide dependent on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. Their minds are neither within, nor without, nor in between the two.
The mind does not take dharmas as its object, nor does it take wisdom as its object; it does not abide in the three periods of time, nor does it abide apart from the three periods of time.

“Venerable sir, you should know that these bodhisattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), do not grasp at a single dharma. Because their mental activity is pure through unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all dharmas, they see all dharmas as entirely stainless. They do not grasp at the signs of seeing; they see without discrimination and remain free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).”

“Venerable sir, you should know that these bodhisattvas, through their skillful means in practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are neither associated with nor dissociated from the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, or the buddha eye; likewise, they are neither associated with nor dissociated from the various knowledges of the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, the supernormal power of the base of psychic power, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.”

“Venerable sir, you should know that the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is neither associated with nor dissociated from any phenomena (*dharma*).”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, attain the knowledge of equality regarding all phenomena; they are able to observe the mental activities of all sentient beings and know all that is defiled and pure exactly as it is. Furthermore, they do not lose mindfulness of the immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha.

These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), attain mastery over all phenomena through effortless mental application. They abide perpetually in silent meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without the functioning of mind, intellect, or consciousness; yet, without arising from this concentration, they teach and transform sentient beings. Performing the works of a Buddha without ever ceasing, they have attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all Buddha-dharmas, their minds being free from attachment or defilement.

For example, it is like a transformation Buddha creating a manifested Tathāgata; that manifested Tathāgata has no mind, thought, or consciousness; no body and no bodily action; no speech and no verbal action; and no mental faculty and no mental action, yet he is able to perform all the works of a Buddha to benefit sentient beings.
Why is this? It is due to the spiritual power of the Buddha.

Thus, through the skillful means of practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattva manifests emanations that are without body and without bodily action, without speech and without vocal action, and without mind and without mental action; yet, without the exertion of effort, they constantly perform the work of a Buddha to benefit sentient beings.

Why is this? Śāriputra, because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they penetrate the fact that all phenomena are like illusions and so forth, such that their minds are free from discrimination; yet, sentient beings constantly hear them preaching the Dharma.

“Virtuous One, you should know that all the wisdom possessed by these bodhisattvas does not abide in the conditioned, nor does it abide in the unconditioned; it does not abide in the aggregates, the elements, or the sense bases; it does not abide in the internal, the external, or in between the two; it does not abide in the wholesome or the unwholesome, nor in the mundane or the supramundane; it does not abide in the defiled or the pure, the out-flowing or the non-out-flowing, the conditioned or the unconditioned; it does not abide in the three periods of time or in that which transcends the three periods of time; and it does not abide in space, analytical cessation, or non-analytical cessation.”

These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, although their minds are always thus without abiding anywhere, are able to penetrate the nature and characteristics of all phenomena. With unimpeded wisdom and effortless application of mind, they proclaim to all sentient beings that all phenomena are eternally quiescent, yet their work of teaching and transforming them never ceases.
These bodhisattvas possess the power of their past vows, which is so strong that they teach the Dharma to others without effortful mental engagement.
By means of the skillful means of profound prajñāpāramitā, these bodhisattvas are always free from fear.
Why is this? Because the Vajradhara deity constantly follows and guards him whether he is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
"Venerable One, you should know this!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this exposition of the profound perfection of wisdom, is not startled, terrified, or bewildered, and remains free from doubt, it should be known that they have already received the prediction of enlightenment.

Why is this? Because by faithfully accepting the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one draws near to the realm of the Buddhas; through this single-mindedness, one is able to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas.
Because one has realized the Buddha-dharma, one brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings, yet does not perceive sentient beings as distinct from the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? Because, in principle, sentient beings and the Buddha-dharma are non-dual.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 573, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine: Non-Apprehension; Part Six: The Ninth Chapter on Non-Apprehension. At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Subhūti (Sanskrit: *Subhūti*), who asked the Most Victorious One:
"Has the Buddha bestowed the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*) upon King Śūra?"
Vijayin replied,
"Although I have received the prediction, I am still like one in a dream.
At that time, Subhūti asked Vijayin again:
“By what has the Heavenly King received his prediction?
Most Victorious replied,
“Although I have received the prediction, there is nothing attained.”
Sudhīra spoke again:
"One who has nothing to attain—what dharma do they not attain?
Vimalajaya replied:

"Non-apprehension" means not apprehending a self, not apprehending sentient beings, and so on, up to not apprehending a knower or a seer; not apprehending the aggregates, the elements, or the sense bases; whether wholesome or unwholesome, defiled or pure, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, or saṃsāra or nirvāṇa—in all such things, there is nothing to be apprehended.
Sudhi again asked:
"If there is nothing to be attained, what is the use of receiving a prediction [of enlightenment]?
Vīrasena replied:
"Because of non-attainment, one receives the prediction [of enlightenment].
Good Thought asked again:
"If the meaning of what the Heavenly King has said is as you have stated, then there would be two kinds of knowledge:"
"First, there is non-attainment;
second, there is receiving the prediction [of enlightenment].
Most Victorious replied:
“If there were duality, there would be no bestowal of the prediction [of enlightenment]. Why is this?
The wisdom of the Buddha is non-dual; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow the prediction upon bodhisattvas by means of non-dual wisdom.”
Sudhi again asked:
"If wisdom is non-dual, how can there be the bestowing of a prediction and the receiving of a prediction?
Vīrasena replied:
"The prophecy and the recipient of the prophecy are non-dual at their limit.
Suvicintin spoke again:
"If they are non-dual at their limit, how can there be a prophecy?"
The Most Victorious One replied:
"To reach the limit of non-duality is itself to provide a definitive answer.
Suvicintin asked again:
“Great King, abiding now in what limit do you receive this prediction?
Most Victorious replied,
“I receive this prediction while abiding in the limit of the self, the limit of sentient beings, and even the limit of the knower and the seer.”
Sudhi further asked:
"Where should this 'limit of self' and so forth be sought?
Vajrāgra replied:
"One should seek it at the limit of liberation of all Buddhas.
Suvicintin asked again:
"And where, in turn, should one seek the limit of the Buddhas' liberation?"
The Most Victorious One replied:
"One should seek it at the boundary between ignorance and craving for existence.
Subhūti then asked again:
"Where should one seek ignorance and craving?
The Most Victorious One replied,
"One should seek them at the limit of ultimate non-arising."
Sudharma asked again:
"In what, then, should this limit of non-arising be sought?
Vimalajaya replied:
"At this point, one should seek it at the limit of non-knowing.
Subhūti asked again:
"The limit of non-knowing is precisely the absence of anything known; how can one seek this point there?"
The Most Victorious One replied:
"If there is something known, it cannot be found through seeking; because there is no knowing, one seeks within that very limit.
Suvicintin asked again:
"At this juncture, being beyond words, how can it be sought?
Vimalakīrti replied,
"It is precisely because words have ceased that it can be sought."
Sudhi again asked:
"How is this speech to be severed?
Vimalajaya replied:
"Because all phenomena rely on the meaning and not on the words.
Sutasoma then asked:
"In what way do they rely on the meaning?"
The Most Victorious One replied,
“I do not perceive the characteristic of phenomena.
Suvicintin asked again:
"How does one not see? Vimala replied:
"By not giving rise to conceptual discrimination."
"Meaning is that which is relied upon, and I am that which relies upon it.
Because these two things do not exist, it is called 'not seeing.
Sudarśana asked again:
"If one does not perceive any objective referent (artha),
what is there to seek? Vimalakīrti replied,
"Because there is neither seeing nor grasping, it is called 'seeking'."
Sudharma asked again:
"If the Dharma can be sought, does that mean there is seeking?
Vimalajaya replied:
"This principle is not so; for one who seeks the Dharma truly has nothing to seek.
Why is this? If there were truly something to be sought, it would be non-Dharma."
Sudhi again asked:
"What is this Dharma? Varasena replied:
“The Dharma has no letters and is also beyond language.
Suxin asked again,
“Within that which is free from words and letters, what is the Dharma?”
The Most Victorious One replied:
“That which is by nature detached from words and letters, where the sphere of mental activity ceases—this is called the Dharma.

The nature of all phenomena is utterly ineffable; even that ineffability cannot be expressed. Should anything be spoken, it is merely a fabrication; within these fabricated phenomena, there is no real dharma whatsoever.”
Sudhi again asked:
"Do all the words spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas always constitute falsehood?
Vimalajaya replied:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word from beginning to end;
how, then, could there be falsehood? Suxin asked again:
"If there were something spoken, what fault would there be?"
The Most Excellent One replied,
"There is the fault of speech.
Suvicintita asked again:
"What fault is there in speech?
Most Victorious replied,
"There is the fault of conceptualization."
Sudhi again asked:
"What dharma is faultless?
Vīrasena replied:
"If one speaks of existence and non-existence without perceiving these two characteristics, then there is no fault.
Suxi asked again:
"What is the root of this fault?"
The Most Excellent One replied:
"Apprehension is the root.
Subhūti asked again:
"What is the basis of grasping?
Vimalakīrti replied,
"The mind of attachment is the basis."
Sudhi again asked:
"What is the root of attachment?
Vimalajaya replied:
“False conceptualization is the root.
Sudharma then asked:
“What is the root of false conceptualization?”
The Most Victorious One replied:
"Apprehension is the root.
Subhūti asked again:
"What is the object of his focus?
Vimala replied, "He focuses on forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena."
Sudhi again asked:
"What is meant by 'without an object'? Vajra replied:
"If one is free from craving and grasping, there is no object of focus. For this reason, the Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena are equal and cannot be taken as objects of focus.

When this Dharma was spoken, five thousand bhikṣus became free from dust and defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye; furthermore, twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Sujaya rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that when good sons and good daughters hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment are able to do so immediately; how is it that they all achieve non-retrogression and, practicing with constant excellence, never fall back?"
The Buddha said:
"O Heavenly King!
Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Pay close attention, and I shall speak for you.
Most Excellent replied:
“Excellent! Great Sage! Indeed!”
"Please speak!
We long to hear it.
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

“Great King, you should know! If good sons and good daughters hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to the bodhicitta with a pure and sincere mind, possess right faith and draw near to the noble ones, delight in hearing the true Dharma and remain far removed from envy and stinginess, constantly cultivate tranquility and take pleasure in practicing generosity, have a mind free from obstruction and untainted by defilements, possess right faith in the law of karma and its fruits without hesitation, understand the karmic results of black and white deeds as they truly are, and would never commit evil even for the sake of their own bodies or lives—

then these good sons and good daughters, by thus practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will be able to distance themselves from the ten paths of unwholesome action and will always keep the ten paths of wholesome action in mind.”

These sons and daughters of good family, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), if they see śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who are correctly diligent in their practice, pure in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), learned and understanding the meaning [of the teachings], constantly maintaining right mindfulness with a pliant and gentle mind, serene and undisturbed, always speaking words of love, diligently cultivating all that is wholesome and remaining far removed from all that is evil; who are not arrogant toward themselves nor contemptuous of others, who avoid coarse and wicked speech and distance themselves from meaningless talk; who do not abandon the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and whose minds are disciplined and upright; who are able to sever the violent torrents and skillfully extract the poisoned arrows; who are able to cast off all heavy burdens, transcend the states of no leisure (*akṣaṇa*), and cross over beyond further existence (*punarbhava*).

These sons and daughters of good family, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, should, upon seeing this bodhisattva, draw near to him and rely upon him as a virtuous friend.
At that time, this bodhisattva, through skillful means, taught the Dharma to them according to what was appropriate:

"You should know! Those who are able to practice giving shall obtain wealth and happiness; those who uphold the pure precepts shall be born nobly in the heavens; and those who listen to the true Dharma shall attain great wisdom."
He further addressed him, saying:
"This is generosity; this is the fruit of generosity.
This is stinginess; this is the fruit of stinginess."
This is pure ethical discipline, and this is the fruit of pure ethical discipline;
this is the violation of ethical discipline, and this is the fruit of violating ethical discipline;
this is patience, and this is the fruit of patience.
This is anger, and this is the fruit of anger;
this is diligence, and this is the fruit of diligence;
this is laziness, and this is the fruit of laziness.
"This is meditative concentration; this is the fruit of meditative concentration.
This is distraction; this is the fruit of distraction.
This is sublime wisdom; this is the fruit of sublime wisdom."
"This is delusion; this is the fruit of delusion.
This is wholesome bodily action; this is the fruit of wholesome bodily action.
This is unwholesome bodily action; this is the fruit of unwholesome bodily action."
"This speech is wholesome karma; this speech is the fruit of wholesome karma.
This speech is unwholesome karma; this speech is the fruit of unwholesome karma.
This mental action is wholesome karma; this mental action is the fruit of wholesome karma."
"This is mental unwholesome karma; this is the fruit of mental unwholesome karma.
This dharma should be practiced; this dharma should not be practiced.
If one cultivates in this way, it will bring happiness for a long night; if one does not cultivate in this way, one will obtain suffering for a long night."
These sons and daughters of good family, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means and associating with virtuous friends, hear this sequential teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, knowing that this bodhisattva is a vessel for the Dharma, he then proclaims the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, saying:

"Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of volitional effort, non-arising, non-cessation, and the absence of a self, a sentient being—and so on at length—up to the absence of a knower or a viewer."
He further proclaimed for them the profound dependent origination, saying: "Because this dharma exists, that dharma arises; when this dharma ceases, that dharma accordingly ceases. That is to say:

with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; and so on, until: if birth ceases, then old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease."
At that time, this bodhisattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, further spoke thus:
"Within the reality of ultimate truth, there is not a single dharma that can arise or cease."

Why is this? All phenomena in the world arise from causes and conditions; they are devoid of a self, a sentient being, an agent, or an experiencer. It is said that phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and that phenomena cease when causes and conditions disperse. There is not a single real phenomenon that undergoes arising or ceasing.

False conceptualization within the three realms exists merely as a provisional designation; it undergoes the ripening of results according to karma and afflictions. However, if one observes with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as it truly is, then all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, without agent or recipient.
If dharmas are without activity, they are also without formation; thus, the mind has no attachment to any dharmas, namely:

it does not attach to form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; it does not attach to the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; it does not attach to the sense-object of form up to the sense-object of phenomena; it does not attach to the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; it does not attach to the element of form up to the element of phenomena; and it does not attach to the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness.
Then, this bodhisattva further spoke these words:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, quiescent, detached, without grasping, and without attachment."
“Because these sons and daughters of good family speak thus, they practice with constant progress and never fall back.
O Heavenly King, you should know this!”
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, delight in beholding the Buddhas and delight in hearing the true Dharma;
they do not fall into lowly or base states, and in whatever place they are born, they are never separated from seeing the Buddhas and hearing the true Dharma,
making offerings to the Saṃgha, constantly beholding the Buddhas, and being courageous and diligent.
Advancing with resolve to seek the True Dharma, he does not cling to conditioned things such as wife and children or servants;
he is likewise free from greed for the necessities of life and remains untainted by various desires.

Constantly relying on the authentic teaching, he cultivates the recollection of the Buddha, renounces the world to leave the household life, practices according to the instruction, and subsequently explains it to others; yet, though he speaks to others, he seeks no recompense.
