Just as a person with eyes cannot behold any forms in the absence of external light, so too a practitioner, though possessing wisdom, cannot see the Dharma without a virtuous friend."
Just as one with the divine eye can see forms without depending on external light, so too does a bodhisattva who has entered the stream of the Dharma naturally advance.
For example, just as those dwelling within a womb gradually grow yet do not perceive it themselves;
so too, for a bodhisattva who exerts diligent effort, various practices gradually increase without their own perception, yet they are able to accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as there are wondrous medicinal trees upon the Snowy Mountains whose branches, twigs, stems, and trunks neither wither nor break;
so too, when a bodhisattva diligently cultivates vigor, all their sublime practices neither regress nor are lost.

"Just as a wheel-turning monarch appears in the world endowed with the seven treasures, so too does a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of enlightenment become endowed with the seven jewels of the Dharma—namely, generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means."

Just as a wheel-turning monarch travels through the four continents with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, so too does a bodhisattva benefit sentient beings through the four means of attraction, his mind always remaining impartial.
Just as wherever a wheel-turning monarch resides, there is no dispute or litigation, so too, when a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma according to reality, there is no contentious debate.

For example, just as when the trichiliocosm is first formed, there immediately appear Sumeru, the king of mountains, and the great ocean, so too, when a bodhisattva first generates the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, there immediately arise prajñā and great compassion.

For example, when the sun rises, its light first shines upon those mountains that are highest; likewise, when a bodhisattva obtains the torch of prajñā, it first illuminates those bodhisattvas who possess lofty conduct and whose faculties have matured.

Just as the great earth can universally support all grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, and medicinal plants with complete impartiality, so too the bodhisattva who has realized such a dharani-gate maintains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāntamati, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said.

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain such a gateway of dhāraṇīs, then every word and every syllable they speak is none other than the Buddha’s speech; such speech is far removed from form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because this Dharma that is taught is not of the mundane world, it is inexhaustible and boundless, and it can bring about lightness and agility of all body and mind.
Even if one were to preach before hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the speaker would not feel timid or weak.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, has a mind free from attachment—namely, not attached to a self, not attached to sentient beings, and not attached to any phenomena. By means of this, they realize pure *tathatā*, the pure *dharmadhātu*, and the pure *bhūtakoṭi*. They attain inexhaustible Dharma, inexhaustible syllables, and inexhaustible eloquence. At that time, they give rise to a sublime joy because they have attained wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*), attained wondrous knowledge (*jñāna*), and are free from the net of doubt.

When the Buddha spoke this gateway of dhāraṇī, eight thousand bodhisattvas simultaneously attained the dhāraṇī gateway of non-entry into all phenomena; furthermore, twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression, five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), sixteen thousand hosts of devaputras became free from dust and defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye, and immeasurable and boundless sentient beings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāntamati, saying:
"This dhāraṇī is able to subdue the hosts of Māras, destroy all non-Buddhists, and ruin those who harbor envy toward the Dharma."

However, the *Prajñāpradīpa* extinguishes the fire of afflictions and protects the expounder of the Dharma, enabling them to reach nirvana; it subdues the inner mind and skillfully transforms those outside, its dignified demeanor inspiring joy in all who behold it. It expounds the Dharma with impartiality for those practicing correctly, observing the faculties and natures of sentient beings as they truly are, and bestowing the teachings at the appropriate time—neither too early nor too late.
When the Buddha had spoken these words regarding such merits, the great oceans, Sumeru the king of mountains, the great earth, and all the mountains within this trichiliocosm quaked and trembled.

At that time, the heavens rained down exquisite *sūkṣmasvara* flowers, great *sūkṣmasvara* flowers, *maṅgalasvara* flowers, great *maṅgalasvara* flowers, *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *padma* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and *karmara* flowers; meanwhile, the gods in the sky performed various kinds of music.
The World-Honored One again addressed Śāntamati, saying: "Good son!

In the past, immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless inconceivable kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnacandra, fully endowed with the ten titles. His land was named Adūṣya, and his kalpa was named Priyapraśaṃsita. He had thirty-two billion śrāvaka disciples and immeasurable, boundless bodhisattva disciples; yet that Tathāgata realized bodhi without prior ascetic practices or the subduing of Māra."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva among that assembly named Ratnaguṇa, who possessed sublime eloquence and was able to teach the Dharma to sentient beings in various ways.
Then, the great multitude requested that Tathāgata not enter parinirvāṇa, but remain long in the world.
At that time, Ratnaguṇa addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are neither born nor do they perish; why then should one exhort them not to enter nirvana?"
If the great void were to enter nirvāṇa, then the Tathāgata might enter parinirvāṇa;
if true thusness, the dharma-realm, the limit of reality, or the inconceivable realm were to enter nirvāṇa, then the Tathāgata might enter parinirvāṇa.

Why is this? Because the Dharma of the Tathāgata is neither formed nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure; it is neither worldly nor supramundane, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, and neither eternal nor annihilated.

Even if one possessed ten tongues in a single mouth, and from each of those tongues a hundred more were produced, and from each of those a thousand more, one still could not describe the formation and destruction of the Tathāgata, nor even speak of permanence or annihilation; how then can the great assembly entreat the Tathāgata not to enter parinirvāṇa but to remain long in the world?

When that Jewel-Virtue (Ratnaguṇa) preached this Dharma, eighty-six thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression; seven thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously attained the dharanī-gate of boundless merit, the dharanī-gate of pleasing the mind, the dharanī-gate of non-obstruction, the dharanī-gate of joy, the dharanī-gate of great compassion, the dharanī-gate of moon-love, the dharanī-gate of moonlight, the dharanī-gate of sun-love, the dharanī-gate of sunlight, the dharanī-gate of the King of Mount Sumeru, the dharanī-gate of the deep and vast great ocean, and the dharanī-gate of the jewel-king of merit. Furthermore, thirty-six thousand people from the great assembly of devas became free from dust and removed from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye.
The Blessed One again addressed Śāntamati, saying:
"In the past you were Ratnaguṇa; it is by virtue of this cause and condition that you are able to speak of the various merits of this dharanī gateway."
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī spoke these verses:
“Dhāraṇī is like a wondrous medicine, Able to cure the diseases of manifold delusions;
It is also like the celestial nectar of immortality, Which brings constant peace and bliss to those who consume it.”
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King Puṇyapuṣpa spoke again in verse:
“Dhāraṇī is without letters, yet letters manifest dhāraṇī;
Through Prajñā and great compassion, that which is beyond words is expressed by words.”

At that time, the Heavenly King Śāntuṣita rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The merits of all Buddhas are inconceivable; the teachings spoken by all Buddhas are inconceivable; and the sublime practices performed and the wondrous Dharma taught by the great Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.”
"The roots of goodness we gods have planted in past lives are profound and deep, such that we have encountered the Tathāgata and heard him preach such a profound and wondrous Dharma.
Thereupon, they scattered immeasurable celestial flowers and incense over the Tathāgata as an offering.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"Heavenly King, you should know!
Those who wish to make offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, should cultivate three dharmas: [text continues]"
First, to resolve upon bodhicitta;
second, to protect and uphold the true Dharma;
third, to practice according to the teachings.
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
If one can cultivate and study these three dharmas, they may be called a true供养 (pūjā) of the Buddha.
Even if the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa and speak of the merit obtained from this offering, he could not exhaustively describe it."
Therefore, O Heavenly King!
If one wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possessing these three dharmas constitutes true offering.
O Heavenly King, you should know this!
If one protects even a single four-line verse of the Buddha, one thereby protects the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, arises from the Dharma.
Thus, the offering of the Dharma is called the true offering; it is the foremost among all offerings, such that material offerings cannot compare to it.
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
I recall that in the past, during immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable eons while I was diligently practicing and studying the bodhisattva path, I heard a deity in the sky recite this verse:
'Two people are far removed from kings, thieves, and the like— They are a great treasure-store that cannot be plundered.'"
The Dharma is difficult to hear in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; though one may hear it, they do not uphold it nor practice its giving.

To protect the True Dharma with the Great Bodhicitta, to practice according to the teachings with a tranquil mind, and to maintain an impartial mind that benefits both self and others—this is what is called the true offering to the Buddha.
"O Heavenly King, you should know!

When I first heard this verse in the past, I immediately recited it for others; at that time, eight thousand sentient beings together gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Therefore, O Heavenly King!
Making offerings through the Dharma is the most supreme. Why is this so?
“Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is born from the Dharma.

Chapter 14: Exhortation, Part Six, Chapter Fourteen, Section One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose again from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Tathāgata, will there be any sentient beings in the future age, during the period when the True Dharma is about to perish, who are able to believe and accept it?”
“If good sons, good daughters, and others, upon hearing this sutra preached, believe and accept it without slandering it, what kind of merit will such persons achieve?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!

In a future age, when the period of the decline of the True Dharma is unfolding, there will be sons and daughters of good family who have practiced pure ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas; these true children of the Buddha will be able to believe in this sutra, and the merit they thereby produce will be beyond measure or calculation.
All supreme and wholesome dharmas are born from prajñā. If there are those who can believe and accept this without slandering it, I shall now briefly explain it for you through a parable. "Mañjuśrī!
This Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in circumference; it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a carriage box, and the faces of the people within it are likewise so formed.

Suppose this Jambudvīpa were completely filled with stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, packed together without any gaps, like a grove of millet, rice, sesame, bamboo, reeds, rushes, or sugarcane.

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the entire duration of the lifespan of those noble ones—whether long or short—arouse a profound and pure mind and offer them the finest food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicines available in the world as acts of service and support.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 572. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Six: Chapter Fourteen on Exhortation and Admonition, Section Two. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"Suppose this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds were all ground into the finest atoms, and each individual atom were made into a noble one."

"If sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, circulate, and expound this sutra, the mass of merit they obtain will surpass the merit of the aforementioned giving by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even by an upaniṣad-fold."

“Mañjuśrī! Because they dedicate [their merit] toward seeking all-knowledge, they are able to accomplish the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because those evil sentient beings have such heavy karmic offenses, they are still unable to escape the suffering of the great hells.

Mañjuśrī! Among those evil sentient beings in the Avīci Hell throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not one who has not experienced suffering for many kalpas; how much more so for those in other hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts!
Why is this? Because those deluded ones destroy the Dharma-body mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Even if they were to undergo heavy suffering for as many eons as there are atoms in that sutra, and were subsequently to emerge from the three evil realms and be reborn among humans, they would contract a grave and malignant disease that no physician or medicine can cure.

Even if I were to remain in the world for an eon or more than an eon through my supernatural power, I could not exhaustively describe the retributive consequences of the sins of those sentient beings who slander and obstruct this sutra.
“Mañjuśrī! All wise ones who desire peace and happiness in the present and the future must not slander or obstruct this sutra.
Chapter 15: The Chapter on the Two Practices, Part Six of the Fifteenth Chapter. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he should accomplish the preceding and succeeding perfections of wisdom.”
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have two kinds of practice:
the accomplishment of prajñā and the transformation and guidance of sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish prajñā and transform and guide sentient beings?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, from the beginning of wisdom until the ultimate limit, remains free from the exertion of mental effort while teaching the Dharma inexhaustibly and without interruption—thereby causing sentient beings to escape the evil destinies and the three realms of existence and dwell in the happy destinies, or to realize the noble fruits of the three vehicles."
Mañjuśrī! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom for the purpose of transforming and guiding sentient beings. Mañjuśrī!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and accomplishes boundless, unconditioned wisdom, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s own practice of wisdom.
"Why is this? Because it is able to bring all virtues to perfection.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, what kind of dharma-practice do they cultivate that can correspond with omniscience?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and cultivates the true dharma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they abide in a mode of being that is remote from conceptual thought, subtle, signless, and profoundly deep; it is beyond observation and extremely difficult to penetrate, eternally quiescent, cool, and all-pervading; it is without discrimination, non-attachment, and unimpeded; it accords with correct principle and cannot be grasped; it is utterly still and great tranquility, supreme and peerless among all dharmas.
Mañjuśrī! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, cultivating this dharma-practice enables them to be in accord with all-knowledge.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what sphere do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must resolutely practice the profound perfection of wisdom within the profound realm, the vast realm, and the realm of merit.”

Mañjuśrī! That which is the profound realm has an essence that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it does not cling to the two extremes, nor is it separate from them. Its self-nature is pure, liberated from all obscurations, inconceivable, and beyond measure; it is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Mañjuśrī! That which is the vast object consists of all the merits of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas; it has the two dharmas of great compassion and prajñā as its nature. Free from the marks of conceptual discrimination, it functions without effort, never for a moment ceasing to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings, and all the teachings it proclaims accord with their inclinations.

Mañjuśrī! As for the sphere of merit, it consists of all the merits associated with the practice of profound *prajñāpāramitā* by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

In accordance with the faculties, desires, natures, and conducts of sentient beings, and according to the various distinctions of forms they delight in, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is able to manifest them all. That is to say: he may manifest ascending to Tuṣita Heaven; or manifest descending from heaven to be born in Jambudvīpa; or manifest dwelling in the womb; or manifest his initial birth; or manifest as a youth; or manifest sporting; or manifest leaving home; or manifest practicing austerities; or manifest proceeding to the foot of the Bodhi tree; or manifest realizing unsurpassed enlightenment; or manifest turning the wheel of Dharma; or manifest entering parinirvāṇa. Such manifestations of various distinct forms are all for the sake of liberating sentient beings from birth and death.
“Mañjuśrī! This is called the sphere of activity of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed,
World-Honored One!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattvas is the inconceivable domain of the Buddhas.”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
This profound perfection of wisdom is an uncommon dharma and is inconceivable. Why is this?
All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas cannot penetrate it, for it is not their domain; none except the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are able to attain it. Why is this?

Because the meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is profoundly deep, it is subsumed within the sovereign, immovable, and untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), bringing to full completion the benefit and happiness of sentient beings. Therefore, it is called the sphere of the Buddhas, which transcends the path of language and is subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is far removed from discursive thought, investigation, conceptualization, and deliberation; it cannot be compared by means of worldly dharmas; it is the most supreme among all dharmas; and it neither abides in saṃsāra nor dwells in nirvāṇa.
“Mañjuśrī! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there are five inconceivable matters:
first, their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).”
Second, spatial location;
third, various abodes;
fourth, identity and difference.
Fifth is benefit and happiness.
"Mañjuśrī! In what way is its intrinsic nature inconceivable?"

True thusness (*tathatā*) in form cannot be found by seeking it; true thusness apart from form cannot be found by seeking it. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

True thusness in the eye cannot be found by seeking it; true thusness apart from the eye cannot be found by seeking it. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. True thusness in form cannot be found by seeking it;
true thusness apart from form cannot be found by seeking it. It is the same for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena.

One cannot find the suchness of visual consciousness by seeking it within it, nor can one find it apart from the suchness of visual consciousness; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness.

One cannot find the suchness of the earth element by seeking it within it, nor can one find it apart from the suchness of the earth element; the same applies to the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

One cannot find the suchness of existent phenomena by seeking it within them, nor can one find the suchness of non-existent phenomena by seeking it within them; therefore, their intrinsic nature is inconceivable.
“Mañjuśrī! In what way is it inconceivable?

Such a Tathatā (Thusness) is inconceivable whether it exists within the desire realm, or it is inconceivable if it is apart from the desire realm; it is likewise so for the form realm and the formless realm.”

If it is inconceivable in the eastern direction, and if it is inconceivable apart from the eastern direction, and likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—therefore, the locations of the directions are inconceivable.
“Mañjuśrī! In what way are all dwellings inconceivable?

If dwelling in bliss is inconceivable, if dwelling in tranquility is inconceivable, if dwelling with mind is inconceivable, and if dwelling without mind is inconceivable, for these reasons all dwellings are inconceivable.”
“Mañjuśrī! Why are oneness and difference inconceivable?

The Tathāgatas of the three times are together in one place, subsumed within the naturally pure, untainted realm; whether they are one or different is inconceivable. Therefore, oneness and difference are inconceivable.”
“Mañjuśrī! How is it that benefit and happiness are inconceivable?

Wisdom and spiritual power are one with the single dharma-realm; wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) are equal in their two aspects. They are able to bring about immeasurable benefit and happiness for sentient beings—beyond description and transcending the realm of language—yet they accord with the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings by providing various teachings and various manifestations.”
"The thirty-two marks and eighty secondary signs can all be manifested according to the minds of sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are called the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son!"

The marks and secondary characteristics of the Tathāgata are immeasurable and boundless; if I were to explain them in detail, they could not be exhausted. However, in accordance with what the world delights in, I shall briefly describe the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
“Mañjuśrī! What are called the thirty-two marks?

The soles of the Tathāgata’s feet possess the mark of being level and full, resting with exquisite stability like the base of a casket. Although the ground may be uneven, wherever his feet tread, it becomes entirely level, touching the earth without any variation. This is the first.
The Tathāgata’s soles bear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel, with its rim, hub, and all other characteristics perfectly complete; this is the second.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet are entirely soft and supple, like *tūla* cotton, surpassing all others; this is the third.
The fingers and toes of the Tathāgata’s hands and feet are all slender and long; their perfect and wondrous form surpasses that of ordinary men, signifying longevity—this is the fourth.

Between each of the fingers and toes of the Tathāgata’s hands and feet, there are webbed membranes like those of a king of geese; they are golden, interlaced with patterns as exquisite as fine embroidery—this is the fifth.
The Tathāgata’s heels are broad, long, and perfectly rounded, being in proportion to his insteps and surpassing those of all other sentient beings; this is the sixth.
The Tathāgata’s insteps are high, full, soft, and exquisite, being in proportion to his heels; this is the seventh.
The Tathāgata’s calves are gradually tapered and rounded, like those of the king of the eṇeya antelope; this is the eighth.
The Tathāgata’s arms are long, straight, and well-rounded; standing upright, they reach his knees like the trunk of an elephant king; this is the ninth.
The Tathāgata’s private parts are concealed within a sheath, like those of a dragon-horse or an elephant king; this is the tenth.
Each pore of the Tathāgata grows a single hair, which is soft, lustrous, deep blue-black, and curls to the right; this is the eleventh.

The hair on the Tathāgata’s head and body all slants upward, curling to the right in elegant spirals; it is soft, lustrous, and deep blue-black, adorning his golden body in a most lovely and pleasing manner. This is the twelfth.
The Tathāgata’s skin is fine, thin, smooth, and supple; dust, grime, water, and the like do not adhere to it—this is the thirteenth.
The Tathāgata’s skin is entirely of a true golden color, radiant and brilliant like a sublime golden pedestal, adorned with various jewels and a sight for all to delight in—this is the fourteenth.
The Tathāgata’s two feet, two hands, palms, neck, and both shoulders—these seven places are full, radiant, pure, soft, and most delightful; this is the fifteenth.
The Tathāgata’s shoulders and neck are perfectly rounded and exquisite; this is the sixteenth.
The Tathāgata’s upper arms and armpits are entirely full and well-developed; this is the seventeenth.
The Tathāgata’s countenance and deportment are grand, full, upright, and straight; this is the eighteenth.
The Tathāgata’s physical form is tall, broad, and dignified; this is the nineteenth.
The Tathāgata’s body is equal in length and breadth, perfectly symmetrical like a nyagrodha tree; this is the twentieth.
The Tathāgata’s neck, chest, and upper body possess a majestic presence as vast as that of a lion king; this is the twenty-first.
The radiance of the Tathāgata’s body extends one fathom in every direction; this is the twenty-second.
The Tathāgata’s forty teeth are even and level, pure and closely set, with deep roots and white as karketana gems or snow; this is the twenty-third.
The Tathāgata’s four canine teeth are brilliant white and sharp; this is the twenty-fourth.

The Tathāgata constantly attains the supreme flavor among all flavors; because the channels of his throat are straight, he can draw forth the supreme flavors from all the channels of the thousand limbs and joints within his body—this is the twenty-fifth.
Twenty-sixth: The Tathāgata’s tongue is thin, pure, broad, and long; it can cover his face up to the hairline at the ears. Twenty-seventh:

The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice is profound and elegant; whether the assembly is large or small, all hear him equally, his voice resonating loudly like a celestial drum, and his speech being graceful and refined like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
The Tathāgata’s eyelashes are like those of a bull king—deep blue-black, even, and not disordered; this is the twenty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s eyes are deep blue-black with a bright white sclera, adorned with a crimson rim that is pure and clearly defined; this is the twenty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s facial disc is like the full moon, and his eyebrows are bright and pure like the bow of Śakra; this is the thirtieth.

Between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows is the white tuft mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which curls to the right and is as soft as *tūla* cotton; its brilliant white radiance surpasses that of conch shells, snow, and the like; this is the thirty-first.
The *uṣṇīṣa* upon the Tathāgata’s crown is lofty, prominent, and perfectly circular, like a celestial canopy; this is the thirty-second.
These are called the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata.
“Mañjuśrī! What are called the eighty minor marks?
The Tathāgata’s fingernails are narrow, long, thin, and supple; they are lustrous, pure, and fresh, like the red copper of a flower—this is the first.
The Tathāgata’s fingers and toes are rounded, slender, and long; they are supple and straight with the joints and bones not visible—this is the second.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet are each equal without disparity, and the spaces between all the fingers and toes are completely filled and dense—this is the third.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet are perfectly rounded and as he wishes, soft, pure, and lustrous, with a color like that of a lotus; this is the fourth.
The Tathāgata’s sinews are coiled and firm, deep-seated and not visible; this is the fifth.
The Tathāgata’s two ankles are both concealed and not visible; this is the sixth.
The Tathāgata’s gait is straight, steady, and composed, like that of a dragon-elephant king; this is the seventh.
The Tathāgata’s gait and majestic bearing are as dignified and solemn as those of a lion king; this is the eighth.
The Tathāgata’s gait is steady, level, and composed, neither overstepping nor falling short, just like that of a bull king; this is the ninth.
The Tathāgata’s manner of walking, advancing, and halting is majestic and dignified, like that of a king of geese; this is the tenth.
When the Tathāgata looks back, he always turns his body to the right, like a royal elephant whose entire body follows the turn of its head; this is the eleventh.
The Tathāgata’s limbs and joints are gradually rounded and perfectly well-proportioned; this is the twelfth.
The Tathāgata’s bones and joints are interconnected without gaps, like the coils of a dragon; this is the thirteenth.
The Tathāgata’s kneecaps are beautifully and excellently positioned, firm and perfectly rounded; this is the fourteenth.
The Tathāgata’s private parts are well-concealed, their lines are exquisite, endowed with majestic power, perfect, and pure; this is the fifteenth.
The limbs of the Tathāgata’s body are supple, soft, radiant, pleasing, fresh, and pure, such that dust and grime do not adhere to them; this is the sixteenth.
The Tathāgata’s physical bearing is dignified and solemn, fearless, and never timid or weak; this is the seventeenth.
The Tathāgata’s limbs are firm, dense, and well-proportioned; this is the eighteenth.
The Tathāgata’s limbs are stable, heavy, and never flickering, being perfectly complete and indestructible; this is the nineteenth.
The physical form of the Tathāgata is like that of a royal seer, perfectly majestic on all sides, radiant, pure, and free from obscurity; this is the twentieth.
The body of the Tathāgata is surrounded by a halo of light, which constantly illuminates him at all times, whether walking or otherwise; this is the twenty-first.
The Tathāgata’s abdomen is square and well-proportioned, without deficiency; it is soft and does not manifest [muscular ridges], being adorned with all the marks—this is the twenty-second.
The Tathāgata’s navel is deep, spiraling to the right, perfectly round and exquisite, pure and lustrous—this is the twenty-third.
The Tathāgata’s navel is thick, neither sunken nor protruding, and is exquisite all around; this is the twenty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s skin is free from scabies and itch, and likewise lacks any blemishes, dark spots, warts, or other such defects; this is the twenty-fifth.
The palms of the Tathāgata’s hands are full and soft, and the soles of his feet are level; this is the twenty-sixth.
The lines on the Tathāgata’s hands are deep, long, clear, straight, glossy, and unbroken; this is the twenty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s lips are lustrous and crimson, like the *bimba* fruit, with upper and lower parts in perfect proportion; this is the twenty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s face is neither too long nor too short, neither too large nor too small, being perfectly dignified and well-proportioned; this is the twenty-ninth.
The tongue of the Tathāgata is soft, thin, broad, and long, with the color of red copper; this is the thirtieth.
The sound emitted by the Tathāgata is majestic, far-reaching, and profound, like the roar of an elephant king, brilliant and clear; this is the thirty-first.
The Tathāgata’s vocal resonance is exquisite and complete, like an echo from a deep valley; this is the thirty-second.
The Tathāgata’s nose is high, long, and straight, with the nostrils not visible; this is the thirty-third.
The Tathāgata’s teeth are even, square, and brilliant white; this is the thirty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s canines are round, white, pure, and gradually tapering to sharp points; this is the thirty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s eyes are pure, with the blue and white clearly distinguished; this is the thirty-sixth.
The Tathāgata’s eyes are long and wide, resembling the petals of a blue lotus and being exceedingly lovely; this is the thirty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s eyelashes are even above and below, dense and not white; this is the thirty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s eyebrows are long and not white, thick yet fine and soft; this is the thirty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s eyebrows are elegantly refined, with a deep blue color like lapis lazuli following its natural sequence; this is the fortieth.
The Tathāgata’s eyebrows are prominent, radiant, and lustrous, shaped like the crescent moon; this is the forty-first.
The Tathāgata’s ears are thick, broad, long, and possess well-formed lobes; this is the forty-second.
The Tathāgata’s two ears are exquisite, even, and free from all defects; this is the forty-third.
The Tathāgata’s deportment enables all who behold him to be free from harm and defilement, giving rise to love and reverence; this is the forty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s forehead is broad, full, level, and upright, with an exceptionally sublime form; this is the forty-fifth.
The upper half of the Tathāgata’s body is perfectly full, majestic and peerless like that of a lion king; this is the forty-sixth.
The Tathāgata’s hair on the head is long, deep blue-black, dense, and not white; this is the forty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s hair on his head is fragrant, pure, fine and soft, lustrous, and curls to the right; this is the forty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s hair on his head is even and orderly, neither disheveled nor entangled; this is the forty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s hair on his head is firm and unbroken, never falling out; this is the fiftieth.
The Tathāgata’s hair on his head is smooth, exquisite, and free from dust or grime; this is the fifty-first.
The Tathāgata’s body is firm and solid, surpassing that of Nārāyaṇa; this is the fifty-second.
The Tathāgata’s body is tall, large, and upright; this is the fifty-third.
The Tathāgata’s apertures are pure, perfect, and excellent; this is the fifty-fourth.
The power and strength of the Tathāgata’s limbs are preeminent and without equal; this is the fifty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s physical marks are such that all who behold them find them pleasing to look upon, never tiring of the sight;
this is the fifty-sixth. The Tathāgata’s facial disc is well-proportioned in its length and breadth, pure and radiant like the full moon in autumn; this is the fifty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s complexion is relaxed and dignified, radiant and manifest; he speaks with a smile, addressing others first rather than turning his back on them—this is the fifty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s countenance is lustrous and serene, far removed from frowning or such defects as a sallow or flushed hue—this is the fifty-ninth.
The limbs of the Tathāgata’s body are pure and stainless, and are forever free from foul odors; this is the sixtieth.
From all the pores of the Tathāgata’s body, there constantly issues forth a subtle and wondrous fragrance that fulfills all wishes; this is the sixty-first.
The Tathāgata’s face constantly emits the most supreme and excellent fragrance; this is the sixty-second.
The Tathāgata’s crown is perfectly round and exquisite, like a madana tree or a celestial canopy; this is the sixty-third.
The hairs on the Tathāgata’s body are deep blue-black, radiant and pure, adorned with red luster like the neck of a peacock, and their color resembles red copper; this is the sixty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-voice accords with the capacity of the assembly, neither increasing nor decreasing, responding to principle without error; this is the sixty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) cannot be seen by anyone; this is the sixty-sixth.
The joints of the Tathāgata’s fingers and toes are distinct and clearly defined, adorned with exquisite beauty like the color of red copper; this is the sixty-seventh.
When the Tathāgata walks, his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground, yet the marks of his footsteps appear; this is the sixty-eighth.
The Tathāgata maintains himself independently without requiring the service of others; his body is without swaying or staggering; this is the sixty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s majestic virtue resounds afar, such that those with evil minds rejoice upon hearing it, while those who see him find peace amidst their fears; this is the seventieth.
The Tathāgata’s voice is neither too high nor too low; he speaks in harmony and with joy according to the inclinations of sentient beings; this is the seventy-first.
Seventy-second: The Tathāgata is able to preach the Dharma in accordance with the speech, sounds, and mental dispositions of all classes of sentient beings. Seventy-third:
When the Tathāgata expounds the sublime Dharma with a single voice, each class of sentient beings understands it according to their own capacity.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma always follows a sequential order and necessarily possesses its causes and conditions; his speech is never unwholesome—this is seventy-fourth.
The Tathāgata regards all classes of sentient beings with impartiality, praising the good and censuring the evil without affection or aversion—this is seventy-fifth.
The Tathāgata acts only after first observing, his conduct being perfectly complete so as to make beings recognize what is wholesome and pure; this is the seventy-sixth.
The marks and signs of the Tathāgata cannot be fully perceived by any sentient being; this is the seventy-seventh.
The cranial bone of the Tathāgata is firm, solid, and perfectly rounded; this is the seventy-eighth.
The countenance of the Tathāgata remains perpetually youthful and does not age, and he delights in visiting his former haunts; this is the seventy-ninth.

On the Tathāgata’s hands, feet, and the area before his chest, there are all the auspicious and joyful svastika marks; their patterns are like exquisite paintings and their color resembles vermilion—this is the eightieth.
"These are called the eighty minor marks of the Tathāgata.

Chapter Sixteen: Praise (The Sixth Division: Chapter on Praise) At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The merits of the Tathāgata are rare, unequaled, and inconceivable; they are no different from those of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
If one has seen the Tathāgata or heard of his merits, such sentient beings are likewise inconceivable.
Now, seeing the Buddha once more turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, they have attained what they never had before and leap for joy with exultation.
Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees and, with palms joined, praised him, saying:
"Among all classes of sentient beings, Only the Buddha is most honored;
Since there is not even one equal to him, How could there ever be one superior?"
Both self and phenomena are empty; the wondrous principle is peerless.
Only I, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, am able to equal that which is peerless.
Afflictions along with their residual habits are both exhausted, forever without remainder.
Able to know all phenomena, there is nothing he does not clearly understand.
Whether in wisdom or in preaching the Dharma, none can equal the Buddha;
throughout the trichiliocosm, the Buddha alone is supreme.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, are certainly real and not false;
they are things that neither Śakra nor Brahmā can ever attain.
Through the great kindness and virtue of the World-Honored One, all sentient beings are universally moistened.
This matter is inconceivable; certainly none can equal it.
By means of subtle and wondrous wisdom, as well as skillful expedients, he transforms and guides all sentient beings, causing them all to obtain benefit and happiness.

At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Wondrous Color (Varṇa). He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
"Those who say there is anyone in the world equal to the Buddha, Their words are not true; they are false and deceptive.
If one says the Dharma King is most supreme and honored, These words are not delusory; they are words of truth."
When the hosts of devas and humans pose their challenges, none are able to refute my Great Teacher;
the Sugata has subdued Māra and conquered the non-Buddhists, leading the world toward liberation.
With pure and inexhaustible eloquence in the four analytical knowledges, you bestow the wondrous medicine of ambrosia upon sentient beings;
universally observing all phenomena with unimpeded wisdom, not a single moment is ever diminished or lost.
With great compassion, he regards all sentient beings with equanimity; his pure mind is unstained by the world.
Skillfully understanding their faculties, desires, and natures, he teaches them according to what they wish to hear.

The distinctions among afflictions are not of a single kind; To demonstrate immeasurable doors of remedial practice, Only the Buddha skillfully explains their causes and conditions, Exclusively for the sake of the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
To encounter a Buddha and hear the Dharma yet fail to attain the noble state—such sentient beings are most difficult to deliver.
One should thirstily yearn for the Great Name of the Tathāgata; if one succeeds in seeing him, the benefit is boundless.
The Buddha’s wisdom can purify the mind; By hearing the true teaching, one transcends birth and death.
Hearing the Buddha’s name brings great auspiciousness; Constantly mindful of the World-Honored One, one is ever joyful.
Having resolved to go to the Buddha, one gives rise to wisdom and understanding; practicing diligently according to the teachings, one accomplishes the knowledge of all modes.
With the category of ethical discipline pure and free from defilement, meditative concentration is supreme and the mind is clear and bright.
Supreme wisdom is most difficult to shake; the ocean of Dharma is pure like nectar.
While all sentient beings delight in heedlessness, the Buddhas remain single-mindedly diligent, transcending the world.
He regards all sentient beings with equal compassion as if they were his only child; his kindness and virtue are so profound that none can repay them.
First, he taught the Dharma capable of destroying the thieves of the fetters, and for a long time he has crushed the illusory armies of devas and māras.
The World-Honored One has already spoken of the faults of the three realms of existence and extensively demonstrated the immeasurable virtues of nirvāṇa;
it is extremely difficult to hear such teachings even in hundreds of thousands of great kalpas, and therefore I now offer praise and prostration with utmost sincerity.

At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Sunāman. He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata practices great compassion with equanimity;
if he were to bestow the wisdom of liberation upon another, he would still let Devadatta be the very first to receive it— how much more so for other classes of sentient beings!”
I now feel no satisfaction in passing my time in vain; I shall cultivate the Great Practice to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Even if one attains the untainted cessation realized only within oneself, they have not yet repaid the Buddha’s kindness;
only if one practices the Buddha’s profound teaching can one be called a true son of the Buddha.
The Buddha long underwent diligent hardships for the sake of sentient beings; his unsurpassed great kindness is rarely repaid.
Through his great compassion, he revealed the true and wondrous Dharma, enabling all to practice it while simultaneously transforming others.
If the Buddha did not appear in the world, all sentient beings would undergo great suffering;
there would be no humans or devas, only the evil realms, and one would hear nothing but the sounds of various kinds of misery.
In all realms of existence, none can escape suffering, for sentient beings are bound by afflictions;
wishing to untie the knots of poison in others, the Buddha is instead entangled by great compassion.
The Tathāgata is the great field of merit for the world; by practicing correctly according to his teachings, one leaves the evil realms behind.
If one violates the Buddha’s teachings and fails to practice, one will certainly not be reborn among humans or devas.
Those who give rise to malice toward the Buddha, or who take no pleasure in hearing the profound Dharma—such sentient beings are truly pitiable; they are certain to dwell forever in darkness.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows through his own wisdom—only one equal to a Tathāgata can fully comprehend it;

the Buddha’s wisdom is beyond my power to measure. I bow my head in reverent salutation to the Buddhas of the ten directions, whose powers of fearlessness and wisdom are unique qualities not shared by others;
these alone are perfectly and fully possessed by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Adorned with the marks and signs, of subtle and wondrous fragrance, Those who behold you never tire;
surpassing all other colors, The three kinds of blossoms unfold without ceasing for a moment— To this pure Buddha-flower, I now pay homage.
Only the Buddha well knows supreme awakening, And is able to forever transcend all perils and hardships;
The Buddha is the foremost and most unsurpassed, I bow my head and take refuge in the Honored One among Two-legged Beings.
With the water of the merit of the True Dharma, the Buddha is able to universally wash away all defilements;
the World-Honored One is inherently pure both within and without—I now prostrate to this body of true purity.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata is fully endowed with supreme merit and wisdom; He benefits and brings joy to sentient beings without a moment’s rest.
Constantly raining down nectar to quench their hunger and thirst, I now bow my head to this one who is able to benefit others.”
Those most supreme and venerable in the world, even they come to make offerings to the Buddha;
with all evils exhausted and all virtues perfected, I now bow my head to the Peerless Honored One.
Universally to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, there is not a single practice he does not cultivate;
causing them to cross over birth and death and attain peace and happiness— I now bow my head in homage to the Teacher who saves the world.
I prostrate to the subtle and wondrous golden body; I prostrate to the nectar-like Dharma that has been taught;
I prostrate to the pure and stainless wisdom; I prostrate to the forest of all meritorious virtues.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Brahmā, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
As you have praised,
this matter of the Tathāgata is true and not false. Why is this?

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have cultivated and accumulated various merits and wisdom; consequently, at this stage of fruition, there is nothing that is not fully perfected. Why is this so?

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; his body, speech, and mind are entirely pure. Therefore, he is able to penetrate suchness and the limit of reality; because he abides in the limit of reality, his words are never false.
At that time, the Great Brahma King prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One, by means of your supernatural powers, will cause this Prajñāpāramitā to abide long in the world for the benefit and happiness of all!”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Brahmā King:

"All Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, by means of their great supernormal powers, together protect and keep in mind this profound Prajñāpāramitā so that it may long abide in the world for the benefit and happiness of all beings; thus, neither celestial Māras, Brahmins, non-Buddhist practitioners, nor śramaṇas shall have the power to destroy or obstruct it."
Why is this? I recall that in the past there was a Buddha named Ratnacandra Tathāgata, whose ten titles were complete; his land was named Adūṣya, and the eon was named Priyapraśaṃsita.

That Buddha had two bhikṣu disciples who served as great Dharma masters and skillfully expounded the profound Dharma: the first was named Jñānavardhana and the second was named Satyadatta. They constantly followed that Buddha as he turned the wheel of the true Dharma, and throughout the course of one kalpa, they proclaimed this most profound *prajñāpāramitā*, whereby three thousand great thousands of koṭis of māras were all transformed and inspired to resolve upon bodhicitta.
"Therefore, no devas, Māras, or others possess the power to destroy or obstruct this sutra.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what place does the Tathāgata Ratnacandra reside?"
"Does he still abide in the world,
or has he already entered parinirvāṇa?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāntamati, saying:
“Good son! To the east of here, passing beyond ten thousand koṭis of Buddha-worlds, there was once a world named Undestroyed (Anupahata), where the Tathāgata’s lifespan was ten thousand kalpas.”

In that Buddha-world, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is constantly taught; there, the various celestial Māras and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are unable to obstruct this sutra, and they all resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The bhikṣu Jñānavardhana is none other than the present Mañjuśrī, and the bhikṣu Satyadatta is none other than the present King Vajradhara; these two bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, have provided manifold protection for the profound Prajñāpāramitā, ensuring that it remains long in the world.

If in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions such profound Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, these two bodhisattvas will immediately go there to hear and receive it; just as they have now gathered here following this light, which was emitted when I preached this Dharma-gate.
17. Chapter on the Entrustment, Part Six: Chapter Seventeen on the Entrustment. At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You should receive and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and do not let it be forgotten or lost!”
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should one receive and uphold such a sutra as this?”
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"There are ten ways to receive and uphold this sutra:
first, transcribing it."
Second, making offerings;
third, giving to others;
fourth, listening attentively.
Fifth, reading and reciting;
sixth, receiving and upholding;
seventh, explaining extensively.
Eighth, recitation;
ninth, reflection;
tenth, cultivation.
By relying on these ten dharmas, one upholds this sutra.
Just as all grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs in the world depend upon the great earth,
so too do all such supreme wholesome dharmas depend upon the Prajñāpāramitā.

Just as the seven treasures constantly appear when a wheel-turning monarch dwells in the world, so too it is with the profound perfection of wisdom: if it dwells in the world, the Three Jewels will not perish.
At that time, the great assembly gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance and, with one voice and in unison, uttered these words of lamentation:

"After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, who will be able to shoulder such a heavy burden of the World-Honored One’s Great Dharma—that unsurpassed Bodhi which was attained through cultivation and accumulation over immeasurable and boundless great kalpas?"

At that time, there were twelve thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly who, in order to protect this Dharma, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence,
spoke these verses: “We renounce our bodies and lives, Seeking no future merit,
To uphold and maintain This profound and essential Dharma taught by the Buddha.”

At that time, five hundred devaputras from within the assembly, with King Bhadra at their head, rose again from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared their left shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, You have perfected the power of the great compassionate vow;
We shall protect and uphold this profound essential Dharma Expounded by the Buddha.”

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and King Vaiśravaṇa all rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One has now proclaimed The subtle and wondrous medicine of Prajñā, Which can cure all illnesses; We shall receive and uphold it upon our heads.”
The Vajrapāṇi deity also rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“The Dharma is fundamentally without name, yet the Buddha has taught it by means of names.
This true teaching of Great Compassion, I now receive upon my head and uphold.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Brahmā Śikhin, saying:
"Brahmā, you should know that the Buddha praises three things as being supreme. What are these three?"
First, to resolve upon bodhicitta;
second, to protect and uphold the true Dharma;
third, to practice according to the teachings.
These three dharmas are the most unsurpassed; those who are able to practice them truly make offerings to the Buddha.
Even if I were to remain in the world for an eon or more than an eon, I could not exhaustively describe these merits.

The merit obtained from upholding even a single four-line verse of the Tathāgata is already inexhaustible; how much more so for upholding the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time!
Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To make an offering of the Dharma is the true offering to the Buddha; offerings of material wealth are not true offerings. Therefore, the offering of the Dharma is the most supreme.
If there are those who protect and uphold the Buddha’s true Dharma, you should know that such persons will enjoy peace and happiness in both worlds.

Therefore, Brahmā, you should always protect the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; by virtue of protecting the Dharma, you shall come to behold all the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa as their respective presiding patrons.

Brahmā, you should know that protecting and upholding the True Dharma in this defiled land for even a brief moment yields greater merit than what would be obtained in a pure land for an entire kalpa or more; therefore, you should diligently protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Blessed One again addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!

Wherever this profound Prajñāpāramitā may be found, you should know that it is the place where the Tathāgata was born, the place where he attained awakening, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and the place where he entered parinirvāṇa."
Why is this? Kausika!
All bodhisattvas, all wholesome dharmas, and all Tathāgatas are born from this.
If there is a Dharma master who proclaims such profound Prajñāpāramitā, this place shall become the domain traversed by the Buddhas;
all sentient beings should, toward that Dharma master, conceive of him as a virtuous friend, generate a mind of reverence for him as a Buddha, and offer him respect, joy, offerings, and praise.
Kauśika, even if I were to remain in the world for an eon or more than an eon, I could not exhaustively describe the merit obtained by this Dharma-preacher who transmits this sutra.
If, wherever this Dharma-master travels, there are sons of good family who are able to prick their own blood to sprinkle upon the ground as an offering, it would not be considered much. Why is this?
"Because the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma is difficult to receive and uphold.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

In future ages, wherever this sutra is preached, I and my retinue shall all provide protection for that place and for the Dharma-preacher; and whenever we behold the location where this sutra resides, we shall immediately give rise to the four kinds of minds previously described.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"That you are able to act in this way is excellent!
Excellent!"
"I entrust this sutra to you; you should protect and propagate it in future ages.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"That we gods have been born in this auspicious realm is entirely due to the *prajñāpāramitā*; the generation of the bodhicitta likewise arises from it. Therefore, disregarding our own bodies and lives, we shall protect such a profound Dharma of the World-Honored One."
At that time, the Buddha again praised Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as has been explained regarding the 'efficient cause'.

Then, when the Bhagavat had finished speaking this sutra, the King of the Most Victorious Heaven, the great bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, all the śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
